sens: Thickness, physical breadth
Wealth, profusion of goods
Generosity in giving
G0100.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the thickness or breadth of a well-developed thing, such as a thick fruit or a vigorous plant — the image of generous growth.
2. Transitioning from the physical to the moral, it signifies wealth or profusion: an abundance of goods, resources.
3. In its only biblical usage preserved, in 2 Corinthians 8:20, Paul uses it to describe the generous collection for the Christians in Jerusalem: he wants to dispel any suspicion regarding the management of this "abundant" offering. The word then evokes the generosity and munificence of the gift.
G0100.origine: The word comes from the Greek hadros, which means "thick, well-formed, vigorous." This is why it is first found with the concrete meaning of "thickness." The suffix -tēs forms an abstract noun: "the state of being thick, ample, rich." This image of growth and breadth naturally extends to the idea of abundance and profusion.
G0100.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament. Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians 8:20 to speak of the collection for the poor of the Church in Jerusalem. He wants to show that he acts with integrity in the management of this generous offering: by using this word, he emphasizes both the breadth ("abundant") and the generosity of the collection, while asserting that no one can doubt his righteousness. It is a rare word, but chosen to magnify the gift and the trust.
G0100.portee: This word reminds the reader that Christian generosity is not small or stingy: it is "abundant," generous, worthy of being entrusted without fear. Paul uses it to show that the material gift of the churches to their brothers is a beautiful and great thing. This encourages the believer to give not out of obligation, but with that generosity of heart that the Bible celebrates.

sens: That cannot be done, that exceeds strength or capacity
That is contrary to natural laws or what was believed possible
Inconceivable, that seems unimaginable
G0101.detail:
1. The word describes what cannot happen or be realized: what exceeds someone's strength or goes against reason. In Matthew 17:20, Jesus says that if the disciples had faith, nothing would be impossible for them — meaning that with faith, even moving a mountain would not be beyond what can be done.
2. It especially refers to what seems contrary to the laws of the world as we know it, what should not happen naturally. Luke 1:37 expresses this perfectly: "Nothing is impossible with God" — this means that God can do what no human creature can imagine, such as giving a child to an elderly woman.
3. The word can also qualify what seems so implausible that one cannot even conceive it, as it appears unreal.
G0101.origine: The word comes from α ("not") added to δυνατός ("powerful, capable"). Literally, it means "not-capable," "without power." It is the direct opposite of the word that means "possible" or "that can be done." The negative prefix α often appears in Greek to create opposites.
G0101.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, always to express the impossible. In Matthew 17:20, Jesus links the impossible to faith: if you had faith, nothing would be impossible, suggesting that faith opens doors that human nature closes. In Luke 1:37, the archangel tells Mary that nothing is impossible with God: this is an affirmation of divine omnipotence in the face of what seems humanly unachievable. In both cases, the word highlights the contrast between human limitations and divine power, or between unbelief and faith.
G0101.portee: This word reminds the Christian that the boundaries of the possible are not where he thinks they are. What seems humanly impossible can be realized through faith in God, whose power is never hindered by the laws of nature. This invites one not to limit God in prayer: what one deems impossible, God can accomplish.

sens: That cannot walk, that is without physical strength
That cannot be done, that exceeds human strength
What only God can accomplish
G0102.detail:
1. The word first describes a person deprived of strength or physical ability: the man sitting in Lystra, "crippled in his feet, lame from birth," cannot walk (Acts 14:8). It is the concrete incapacity of the body.

2. Applied to things or actions, it means that they cannot occur by ordinary means: keeping the Law is "impossible" for the flesh, even though the Law itself is just (Romans 8:3); it is "impossible" for men to save their own souls, but possible for God (Luke 18:27).

3. The word reveals human limits in the face of the absolute: "With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible" (Matthew 19:26). It emphasizes that what exceeds man never exceeds God.
G0102.origine: The Greek word comes from the negation ἀ- ("not") and from δύναμις ("strength, power"). It thus depicts one or that which is without strength. It is found in the Greek translations of the Old Testament to convey the idea of infirmity or powerlessness, particularly when speaking of the poor or the weak.
G0102.emploi: The word appears ten times in biblical Greek. Applied to people, it designates one who lacks physical strength (Acts 14:8) or one who cannot accomplish certain things by their own will (Romans 15:1, where the "weak" contrasts with the "strong"). Applied to things or actions, it expresses radical impossibility: the Law cannot justify (Romans 8:3), dead works cannot purify the conscience (Hebrews 10:4), and those who have tasted certain spiritual experiences cannot be renewed (Hebrews 6:4). The recurring phrase in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) "impossible for men... possible for God" shows that this word primarily reveals the distance between human weakness and divine omnipotence.
G0102.portee: This word teaches the believer a lesson in humility and faith: recognizing that certain things are impossible for him presses him to rely on God rather than on his own strength. Jesus uses it to show that salvation does not come from human effort, but from divine grace. For the one who is weak, physically or morally, the word opens the door: what is impossible for man can become possible in God.

sens: produire des sons mélodiques avec la voix
célébrer ou louer par le chant
exprimer une louange musicale à Dieu
G0103.detail:
1. The word refers to the simple action of producing a melody with the voice. It is a concrete and joyful act: Revelation 5:9 clearly shows this, where heavenly beings "sang a new song." 
2. Singing here is inseparable from celebration and praise. In Ephesians 5:19, the Apostle Paul urges believers to "speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making music from your heart to the Lord": singing is a way to praise together. 
3. Singing becomes the expression of faith and worship towards God. In Colossians 3:16, singing "to God in your hearts" means that musical praise springs from the heart, filled with the word of Christ. It is an act of inner as well as outer worship, where the song of Moses and the Lamb (Revelation 15:3) expresses gratitude for God's works and ways.
G0103.origine: The Greek word ἄδω (adō) is the Athenian form of an older root. It is related to the noun ᾠδή (ōdē), which means "song" or "hymn." This family of words evokes the idea of modulation of the voice, of melody. In the Greek Old Testament, the verb primarily translates the Hebrew שִׁיר (shir), which carries the same meaning of singing praises.
G0103.emploi: The verb appears five times in the New Testament, concentrated in Paul's epistles (Ephesians, Colossians) and in Revelation. In Ephesians 5:19 and Colossians 3:16, it describes the practice of the Christian assembly: believers sing psalms and spiritual hymns to one another, which strengthens their fellowship and instruction. In Revelation 5:9, 14:3, and 15:3, the verb evokes heavenly singing: beings around the throne of God and the redeemed sing new songs and the song of Moses. This heavenly song expresses worship, gratitude, and final victory. The context is always that of liturgical praise or worship.
G0103.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that singing is not a luxury in the church, but a biblical practice of worship and mutual edification. Singing God's praise is to unite one's voice with that of the earthly assembly and, ultimately, with that of all heavenly creatures. Singing thus becomes a living expression of faith, touching the heart, soul, and spirit.

sens: sans interruption, continuellement
à chaque occasion, régulièrement
constamment, perpétuellement
G0104.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: an action that never ceases, that continues without interruption. In 2 Corinthians 4:11, Paul says that the apostles are "always being given over to death" — it is a continuous, permanent state. Hebrews 3:10 speaks of a heart that "goes astray" constantly, never finding stability.

2. A habitual repetition, something that occurs every time, regularly. Mark 15:8 refers to what Pilate "was accustomed" to do at each feast — a recurring practice. 2 Peter 1:12 states that Paul was prepared to remind his readers "continually" of certain things: he does so at every opportunity.

3. The constant character of a quality or disposition. Titus 1:12 describes the Cretans as "always" liars — it is their habitual nature, what can be expected of them at all times. Acts 7:51 reproaches Israel for "always" opposing the Holy Spirit: generation after generation, the same behavior persists.
G0104.origine: This ancient Greek word expresses the absence of limits in time. It comes from an Indo-European root expressing continuity. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew "תָּמִיד" (tamid), which literally means "perpetual, continuous," or "מֵעוֹלָם" (méolam), "from eternity." It is an adverb found in the earliest Greek texts: simple, direct, inevitable.
G0104.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles. In Acts and the letters of Paul, it describes either a constant opposition to the Holy Spirit (Acts 7:51), or the perpetual reality of Christian suffering (2 Corinthians 4:11), or a joy that persists despite circumstances (2 Corinthians 6:10). It can also denote a repeated habit: in Mark, what the governor "was accustomed" to do. In Peter's epistles, it emphasizes the vigilance and faithfulness that must be maintained "continually." Its use in Titus 1:12, applied to a moral character, shows that it also describes a permanent disposition of the heart.
G0104.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian life requires unwavering faithfulness — constant vigilance (1 Peter 3:15), enduring joy despite trials (2 Corinthians 6:10), a permanent refusal to resist God. It is also a call to not grow weary in prayer, brotherly encouragement, and spiritual growth: actions that must never cease, which form the true texture of a living faith.

sens: Grand oiseau de proie aux ailes puissantes
Vautour (en contexte de charogne)
Créature céleste dans la vision prophétique
Symbole de puissance divine et de protection
G0105.detail:
1. The eagle is a large bird of prey recognizable by its strength, powerful wings, and majestic flight. It is a formidable predator of the skies. In Revelation 4:7, the eagle appears as one of the four living creatures around the throne of God, a symbol of cosmic power.
2. When the Bible speaks of carcasses or dead bodies, "eagle" likely refers to a vulture, the bird that feeds on carrion. In Matthew 24:28 and Luke 17:37, Jesus uses this image to say that wherever the carcass is (a symbol of judgment), there the eagles will gather — meaning that judgment will come with certainty, as visible as the gathering of birds of prey around a dead body.
3. In the visions of Revelation, the eagle embodies a heavenly reality: a living creature around the throne (4:7), an angel proclaiming woes to mankind (8:13), or the protective wings given to the woman fleeing the dragon (12:14).
4. The eagle symbolizes divine power, majesty, and protection — characteristics that God claims for Himself and bestows upon those He defends.
G0105.origine: The Greek word aetos comes from an ancient root designating the ultimate predator. It translates the Hebrew nésher from the Old Testament, this bird that God uses as an image of His own strength. The same root gave rise to the Latin word aquila and our French words "aigle." It is a universal word for naming this king of the skies.
G0105.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, only in Revelation and in the words of Jesus. In Matthew 24:28 and Luke 17:37, it illustrates the parable of judgment: the swift gathering of eagles around a carcass signifies that the Son of Man will inevitably be revealed. In Revelation, the eagle changes context: a living creature of heaven (4:7), a messenger of divine plagues (8:13), or a symbol of the wings that carry and protect God's people (12:14). The prophetic context gives this word a very strong spiritual charge.
G0105.portee: The eagle reminds believers that God is master of all power, master of the heavens themselves. When Jesus speaks of the gathering of eagles over a carcass, He teaches that divine judgment is as inevitable and visible as the appearance of a bird of prey: impossible to miss or evade. And when Revelation shows the eagle carrying a woman into the wilderness, it promises that this all-powerful God protects and nourishes His people to the end. It is an image that elevates the gaze and faith.

sens: Bread or cake prepared without leaven, that is, without a rising agent
The Jewish festival of unleavened bread, celebrated in spring in remembrance of the Exodus
Free from moral or spiritual corruption, pure
G0106.detail:
1. In its literal and primary sense, the word refers to bread or a cake prepared without leaven (the agent that makes the dough rise). It is a dense, unleavened bread that keeps for a long time. The Israelites ate it during their flight from Egypt when there was not enough time to let the dough rise (Matthew 26:17: "The first day of unleavened bread").
2. By extension, "unleavened" refers to the great Jewish festival celebrating this foundational event: the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which lasts several days in spring and coincides with Passover. It commemorates the liberation of the people of Israel from Egyptian slavery (Luke 22:1: "The Feast of Unleavened Bread, called Passover").
3. In a figurative sense, Paul uses the word to call Christians to moral purity: just as one must remove leaven from bread, one must distance oneself from anything that corrupts spiritually. Leaven becomes an image of impurity, deceit, and injustice (1 Corinthians 5:7: "Cleanse out the old leaven").
G0106.origine: The Greek word comes from the root ζύμη (zymè), which means "leaven" or "ferment." The prefix ἀ- means "without" or "absence of." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the corresponding word is מָצָּה (matsa), which refers to the unleavened bread eaten during the Exodus. This dietary practice has become one of the most important Jewish rituals, rooted in the collective memory of the people.
G0106.emploi: The word appears nine times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Gospels and Acts, to speak of the Jewish festival. Matthew, Mark, and Luke all mention "the first day of unleavened bread" (Matthew 26:17, Mark 14:12, Luke 22:7), that is, the official beginning of the celebration. Mark adds that "the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread" was to take place (Mark 14:1), emphasizing that the two names refer to the same event. Luke specifies that this feast "is called Passover" (Luke 22:1). Paul, in his first letter to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 5:7-8), completely changes the scope of the word: he uses "unleavened" not to describe a rite, but as a spiritual metaphor urging Christians to live in moral purity, far from the "old leaven" of malice and deceit.
G0106.portee: For the Christian reader, this word anchors Jesus in his Jewish context: he celebrated this feast every year, and it was during this Passover that he instituted the Lord's Supper. For Paul, the word offers a profound spiritual lesson: just as physical leaven transforms the whole dough, sin corrupts the whole being; the Christian life calls for radical purity. Christ's Passover frees the believer, just as it once freed Israel.

sens: Ancestor of Jesus in the Matthean genealogy
G0107.detail: Azor is a figure in the genealogy of Jesus reported by the Gospel of Matthew. He appears in the line of generations descending from Zerubbabel, the leader of the return from exile. Azor fathered Sadok, thus placing him in the royal and priestly lineage that leads to Jesus Christ.
G0107.origine: The name Azor appears only in the New Testament, in the genealogy of Matthew 1. It is not attested anywhere else in the Hebrew or Greek Bible. The context suggests that he is a member of the house of Judah who returned from Babylonian exile, being part of the historical continuity of the people of Israel leading to the coming of the Messiah.
G0107.emploi: Azor appears only twice in the Bible, both in Matthew 1:13-14, in the genealogical list that establishes the legal descent of Jesus according to the flesh. He is presented simply by his name, without epithet or detail, as a link in the genealogical chain. Matthew lists fourteen generations from David to Babylon, and Azor fits into the post-exilic period, representing the continuity of the messianic line despite captivity.
G0107.portee: The mention of Azor reminds the reader that Jesus is rooted in the concrete history of Israel, in an attested genealogy. It underscores God's faithfulness to His promises to the house of David, even after exile and historical ruptures. It is a testimony to the earthly kingship of Jesus, son of David, anchored in historical and genealogical reality.

sens: Philistine city on the Palestinian coast
Place of passage for the apostle Philip after his encounter with the Ethiopian eunuch
G0108.detail: Azotus is the Greek name of an ancient Philistine city located on the Mediterranean coast in the Promised Land. It is here that Philip is miraculously transported after his conversation with the eunuch of Candace (Acts 8:40), where he continues his evangelistic ministry heading toward Caesarea.
G0108.origine: The Greek name Azōtos transcribes the Hebrew name Ashdod (אַשְׁדּוֹד), one of the five major cities of the Philistines mentioned in the Old Testament. This place, rooted in biblical history, bears the same name in the New Testament, testifying to the continuity of human settlements in the Holy Land.
G0108.emploi: Azotus appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 8:40. It is the point of passage for Philip after the Holy Spirit has taken him away from the road where he was speaking with the Ethiopian eunuch. From there, he continues his evangelistic journey to Caesarea, visiting and preaching in all the intervening towns. This place name marks an important step in the expansion of the Gospel beyond Jerusalem.

sens: the atmosphere that surrounds the earth
the empty space, the void
the spiritual realm of demonic powers
the visible sky, the firmament
G0109.detail:
1. Air in its primary sense: the atmosphere we breathe and see around us. Acts 22:23 speaks of dust thrown "into the air" — this is the air we see when we look up. Revelation 9:2 describes the sun and the air darkened by smoke: again, the visible atmosphere that covers the earth.
2. Air in the sense of emptiness or void, without effect or meaning. When Paul strikes "into the air" (1 Corinthians 9:26), he strikes at nothing, without hitting the opponent. When we speak "into the air" (1 Corinthians 14:9), the words are lost without being understood — they go nowhere.
3. Air as the realm of evil powers. Ephesians 2:2 speaks of the "prince of the power of the air": this is the intermediate heaven, the space between the earth and the heaven of God, where Satan and his demons exercise their power. This is why spiritual warfare rages there.
4. Air or the airs as the heaven where believers are taken up. 1 Thessalonians 4:17 describes the faithful taken up "on clouds, to meet the Lord in the air" — this is the visible heaven, the firmament where the glorious meeting will take place.
G0109.origine: The Greek word aēr comes from an ancient root simply designating the air that breathes around us, the lowest atmosphere, the one we can see and feel. The Greeks distinguished aēr (lower, troubled air) from aithēr (pure ether of the divine heights). In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew "shachaq" which also evokes the atmosphere, the visible sky. Nowhere does the Bible borrow from Greek mythology; it simply takes this common term to speak of the space that surrounds us and its spiritual realities.
G0109.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul and in Revelation. Acts 22:23 and Revelation 9:2 use it in its primary and visible sense: the atmosphere where dust flies, where smoke spreads. 1 Corinthians 9:26 and 14:9 play on the idea of empty air and without effect: striking the air means wearing oneself out without result; speaking into the air means being misunderstood. Ephesians 2:2 reveals a hidden reality: the air is also the territory of a demonic authority, the invisible battlefield of the believer. 1 Thessalonians 4:17 and Revelation 16:17 show it as the place of the future glorious manifestation, where Jesus will appear and where the Church will meet Him. No usage is abstract or purely philosophical: the air remains always concrete.
G0109.portee: This word teaches the reader that the visible and the invisible touch each other. When Paul strikes "into the air" or speaks "into the air", he reminds us that a prayer without faith, a word without clarity, an action without a target leads nowhere: one must aim true. Ephesians 2:2 also reveals that the believer faces not only visible enemies but real spiritual powers that occupy the space between us and heaven. Finally, 1 Thessalonians 4:17 anchors hope: one day, the faithful will leave this earth to meet the Lord in the very air, which means that heaven is not far away but close, and that Jesus' promise is not a vague dream but a certain future reality.

sens: State of one who cannot die, who lives eternally
Quality belonging to God alone by nature
Eternal life promised to resurrected believers
G0110.detail: 1. Immortality is the state of one who escapes death and lives without end. The word expresses the absence of death: it is to live forever. In 1 Corinthians 15:53-54, Paul speaks of the moment when our mortal bodies will "put on" immortality — that is, at the moment of resurrection, our bodies will become incorruptible and will no longer be able to die. 2. Immortality is a divine perfection that God alone possesses by nature. In 1 Timothy 6:16, Paul affirms that God alone "has immortality": it is a unique trait of His essence, which radically distinguishes Him from any creature that is born and dies. 3. For believers, immortality is not natural but given: it is the promise of eternal life without death when Jesus raises the dead. It crowns the Christian hope of salvation.
G0110.origine: The Greek word comes from the prefix "a-" (absence, negation) and "thanatos" (death): literally "the absence of death". The root "thanatos" designates death as an inevitable event. Immortality is therefore the negation of this mortal destiny. This term expresses the biblical idea that only God, by nature, cannot die, and that eternal life is the supreme gift He offers to the resurrected.
G0110.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in a context of resurrection and eschatology (the last things). In 1 Corinthians 15, Paul explains how at the general resurrection, mortal bodies will receive immortality — a radical change where death, the ultimate enemy, will be defeated. In 1 Timothy 6:16, the word refers rather to the natural and eternal immortality of God Himself. Christian immortality is therefore a future gift, while that of God is present and essential.
G0110.portee: For the Christian, this word revives the hope of the last things: death will not have the final word. The promised immortality is not a vague spiritual abstraction, but the concrete promise that our bodies will be resurrected and will live eternally with Christ. This transforms our view of death, which loses its definitive character and becomes a passage to eternal glory.

sens: Contrary to established rules, custom, or law
Illegal, something one is not allowed to do
That which violates justice or moral order
G0111.detail:
1. The word describes what goes against recognized and established customs — what people normally do not do. In Acts 10:28, Peter explains to Cornelius that it is "forbidden" for a Jew to associate with a Gentile or enter his house: this is not written in the Law of Moses, but it has become a very strong custom, a rule of the Jewish community.
2. The word also applies to actions that are simply prohibited or criminal — things one should not do. In 1 Peter 4:3, the "excesses" and "criminal idolatries" that Christians have abandoned are things that should simply not be practiced: they transgress moral order and the will of God.
3. At its root, the word expresses the idea of a violation: something that does not fit with what is just, orderly, and proper.
G0111.origine: The word comes from the Greek root θέμις (themis), which designates custom, established law, the recognized order of things. The prefix ἀ- (a-) means "not" or "without". Thus ἀθέμιτος literally means "without established right", "contrary to order". It is a later form of Greek that reinforces the idea of prohibition or illegality.
G0111.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Acts 10:28, Peter uses it to speak of the separation between Jews and Gentiles — a cultural and religious barrier that God's vision has just challenged. In 1 Peter 4:3, the apostle thus qualifies the pagan practices (debauchery, idolatry) that Christians must reject. In both cases, the word marks something that is either culturally forbidden or morally unacceptable.
G0111.portee: This word helps the Christian see that "forbidden" can mean two things: a simple human custom (like the separation between Jews and Gentiles), which can be questioned by God, or a true moral transgression. It invites us to distinguish between human traditions and the true moral principles that God defends. It is a lesson in freedom: what seems "forbidden" is not always contrary to God's will.

sens: Devoid of the knowledge of God
Stranger to God's promises and covenants
Spiritual orphan, abandoned by God
G0112.detail:
1. The word designates one who does not know God, who lives outside any relationship with Him. It is the condition of one who has not received the revelation of the true God. In Ephesians 2:12, Paul uses it to describe the state of the Gentiles before their conversion: they live "without God in the world."

2. To be without God is to be cut off from the covenants and promises that God has made to His people. It is to lack spiritual inheritance, citizenship in the kingdom of God. The text in Ephesians specifies: the Gentiles were "strangers to the covenants of promise."

3. It is a form of spiritual desolation: one who is without God is also without hope, since all true hope rests on God. The word expresses abandonment, not due to God's fault, but due to the ignorance and distance of those who do not know Him.
G0112.origine: The word comes from the privative prefix ἀ- (which means "without") and the word θεός (God). This simple composition is very clear: literally, "without-god." The Greek word takes up an expression coined by the ancients to designate the unbelievers and the wicked, but in the New Testament, Paul applies it to the condition of the Gentiles before the knowledge of the true God, without connotation of moral guilt, but rather of historical ignorance.
G0112.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 2:12, in the context of the unity of the Church and the reconciliation between Jews and Gentiles. Paul reminds the Christians in Ephesus of their previous condition: they lived without God, that is, outside the people of the covenant and its promises. This passage shows how the death and resurrection of Christ changed this situation by granting access to all peoples, without distinction. Paul does not morally condemn the Gentiles; he states a historical fact: before the Gospel, they did not have access to the knowledge of God.
G0112.portee: This word speaks to one who discovers the wonderful gift of having access to God through Christ. It invites the believer to remember where they came from and what they have received: not an acquired right, but a free grace. For the modern Christian, it is also a call to measure their privilege of knowing God and to recognize that this knowledge is never earned or deserved, but offered by divine mercy.

sens: Acting without restraint, without respect for laws and morals
Rejecting divine authority and the norms of conscience
Depraved, given over to passions without limit
G0113.detail:
1. The word describes someone who lives without rules, without moral barriers — as Lot was surrounded by men "unrestrained in their wickedness" (2 Peter 2:7), given over to all forms of immorality. It is the absence of restraint, the refusal of any limit.
2. It particularly designates one who despises natural law — the conscience and order that God has placed in creation — and not just written law. In 2 Peter 3:17, the "ungodly" are those who stray from the Word and live against all authority.
3. The image is that of a beast without a chain, a person abandoned to their own desires without restraint or shame.
G0113.origine: The Greek word comes from θεσμός (themós), which means "law" or "ordinance," with the privative prefix ἀ- (a-) that negates or removes. Literally, it is thus "without law" or "without ordinance." The Hebrew word for "rebellious" or "unrestrained" is similar. The Greek used this term to describe the total absence of moral and legal limits.
G0113.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the second epistle of Peter. In 2 Peter 2:7, it qualifies the inhabitants of Sodom who lived in disorder and debauchery. In 2 Peter 3:17, it designates the false teachers and mockers who reject the Gospel. Peter uses it to warn Christians against those who live without fear of God and lead others into error. The word emphasizes the active contempt for all law — divine and natural.
G0113.portee: This word reminds the reader that a Christian faith life implies a limit, a freely consented obedience to God's law. Seeing the "unrestrained debauchery" of the ungodly is to understand how the Gospel calls us to wisdom and self-control. It is also a warning: to be led astray by such men is to risk losing one's firmness in faith.

sens: To voluntarily set aside, refuse to take into account something (a word, a law, a command)
To annul, render ineffective (a covenant, a plan, a decision)
To push away a person, refuse to listen to or welcome them
G0114.detail:
1. To reject something is to decide not to take it into account, to voluntarily set it aside. It is to refuse to obey an order or to honor a given word. In Mark 7:9, the Pharisees nullify the command of God by preferring to keep their human tradition — they set aside what God has established.
2. To annul means to render completely ineffective, to empty of all value. When one rejects a covenant or a plan of God, one empties it of its power, neutralizes it. In Galatians 2:21, Paul says that he does not reject the grace of God: he does not annul its strength and reality.
3. To reject a person is to push them away, refuse to welcome or listen to them. In Luke 10:16, whoever rejects the apostles rejects Jesus Himself: they set them aside, they close their heart to their message.
4. This rejection can have serious consequences: whoever rejects Jesus and His words will have those words as judge on the last day (John 12:48).
G0114.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb tithêmi which means "to place, to establish." The prefix "a" makes it privative, that is, it expresses the opposite: atheteô thus literally means "not to place, to undo what has been established." That is why the word is used to annul a law, a covenant, or anything that has been put in place. In Hebrew, this verb translates several words that all express rebellion or violation of a covenant: refusing to submit to what has been established as fundamental.
G0114.emploi: This verb appears twelve times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke and in the epistles. It describes the behavior of those who refuse the word of God or the plan of God: the Pharisees nullify the command of God (Mark 7:9), the scribes and elders reject the apostles (Luke 10:16), the ungodly reject the authority of the Lord (Jude 1:8). The word is also used to speak of one who actively sets aside the grace of God (Galatians 2:21) or does not keep their commitment to the Church (1 Timothy 5:12). It is a verb of active and responsible refusal, not simple indifference.
G0114.portee: This word reminds us that our relationship with God and His word is never neutral: we either welcome or reject. To reject what God has established has consequences — it empties of power what was meant to save us. Conversely, not rejecting the grace of God is to acknowledge His authority and love. The word invites the Christian to examine their heart: what do they voluntarily set aside from the teaching of Christ?

sens: Action d'annuler, de rendre sans effet
Suppression, mise de côté d'une loi ou d'une ordonnance
Accomplissement qui rend caduc ce qui précédait
G0115.detail:
1. The word designates the concrete action of canceling something, rendering it null and void. It is like tearing up a contract or declaring it revoked. In Hebrews 7:18, the apostle states that there is an "abolition" of a previous ordinance — that is, the old priestly law is annulled, revoked by what Christ has accomplished.
2. The word is used for the suppression or setting aside of an institution that loses its authority. The system of sacrifices of the old covenant had its usefulness in the past, but it is now abolished, as it did not have the power to make men perfect before God.
3. It is also the fulfillment that renders obsolete what existed before. In Hebrews 9:26, it must be understood that a single sacrifice of Christ "abolishes" sin by permanently removing it. There is no need to return to other sacrifices: they no longer have reason to exist, as the goal has been achieved.
G0115.origine: The word comes from the verb ἀθετέω (athetéô), which literally means "to reject," "to dismiss," "to render ineffective." It is composed of ἀ- (privative: "not") and a root related to establishment or validity. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates Hebrew words that express rebellion, unfaithfulness, or transgression — such as פֶּשַׁע (transgression) or בֶּגֶד (betrayal) — showing that to "abolish" an ordinance is to treat it with defiance, to reject it as invalid.
G0115.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Hebrews. In 7:18, it refers to the abolition of the old priestly law, deemed "powerless and useless." In 9:26, it refers to the abolition of sin by the unique sacrifice of Christ. In both cases, the abolition is not a mere arbitrary suppression, but the fulfillment of a divine plan: what was prefigurative or imperfect gives way to what is definitive and perfect. The context is always that of the transition from the old covenant to the new through the work of Christ.
G0115.portee: This word reminds the believer that Christ did not simply complete or improve the old law: He abolished it, revoked it, substituting it with a new covenant that is infinitely superior. Understanding that one is no longer under the Levitical sacrifices or the ordinances of Sinai frees the Christian from guilt and allows them to grasp that Jesus has had the final word on sin. It is an assurance: in Christ, sin is "abolished," meaning truly dealt with and eliminated, not indefinitely put on hold.

sens: Capitale de la Grèce antique
Ville célèbre pour ses temples, ses philosophes et sa culture
Lieu de rencontre entre l'Évangile et la sagesse grecque
G0116.detail: Athens is the capital of ancient Greece, the political and cultural center of the Greek world. It is a major city during the New Testament period, known for its monuments, schools of philosophy, and intellectual influence. In Acts, Paul arrives there alone after hastily leaving Berea, and "his spirit is provoked by seeing that the city was full of idols" (Acts 17:16) — an expression that shows the clash between the Christian faith and the surrounding idolatry. Paul preaches at the Areopagus, discusses with philosophers, and his companions Silas and Timothy join him (1 Thessalonians 3:1), making Athens a strategic point in his mission in Greece.
G0116.origine: The Greek name Athens (Athēnai) comes from the goddess Athena, the legendary protector of the city. It is plural because the ancient city consisted of several neighborhoods or hills forming an urban ensemble. In classical antiquity, Athens symbolized Greek wisdom, art, and democracy.
G0116.emploi: Athens appears four times in the New Testament, all in the accounts of Paul in Greece (Acts 17-18 and 1 Thessalonians 3:1). It marks a key moment in Paul's mission: it is there that the apostle directly confronts Greek philosophy with the Gospel during his speech at the Areopagus. The passages show Paul waiting for Timothy and Silas in Athens, then leaving for Corinth. The mention of his reaction to the idols highlights the spiritual stakes of this urban stop.
G0116.portee: Athens represents for the Christian the challenge of proclaiming the Gospel in an environment marked by culture, philosophy, and paganism. The passage shows that Paul does not shy away from intellectual dialogue, but submits it to the truth of the risen Christ. It is a reminder that the Christian faith must be embodied in contexts of advanced civilization, without yielding to hidden idolatry.

sens: habitant ou originaire d'Athènes
qui appartient à la ville d'Athènes ou à ses habitants
G0117.detail:
1. The word designates a person born or residing in Athens, the capital of ancient Greece. Paul addresses the Athenians at the Areopagus (Acts 17:22), the hill where magistrates gathered, to announce the Gospel to them.
2. By extension, it qualifies what is specific to Athens or its inhabitants: their customs, their culture, their character. The text notes that the Athenians spent their time listening to the latest news (Acts 17:21), which reveals their intellectual curiosity.
G0117.origine: The Greek word comes from the name of the city, Athens (Ἀθῆναι), and the suffix -αῖος (-aios) which is used to form adjectives of origin or belonging. It is a classical derivative, attested since ancient Greek literature such as Homer's Iliad, to designate the citizens and inhabitants of Athens.
G0117.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's speech in Acts 17 during his visit to Athens. In Acts 17:21, it refers to the inhabitants of the city characterized by their thirst for news and debates. In Acts 17:22, Paul directly uses the term to address his audience at the Areopagus. These two uses show the precise context of Paul's encounter with Greek culture and philosophy in the heart of Athens.
G0117.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of the importance of proclaiming the Gospel in centers of intellectual and cultural power, and how Paul took the time to engage in dialogue with the Athenians, known for their wisdom, using language that resonates with their own culture. It is a model of respect and missionary adaptation in the face of educated listeners who did not know the true God.

sens: Participate in a sports competition, a fight, or a struggle
Face a trial while respecting the rules of the game
Persevere in effort despite difficulty
G0118.detail:
1. The word first evokes the literal sense: to participate in a sports competition, a fight, or a physical struggle. It is the image of games and combats in antiquity, where the athlete engages in a confrontation governed by precise rules.
2. It also means to face a trial while scrupulously adhering to established rules. In 2 Timothy 2:5, the Apostle Paul uses this image: the athlete does not receive the crown of victory unless he has "competed according to the rules" — this alludes to the necessity of fighting according to order and discipline.
3. By extension, it means to persevere in effort with courage and tenacity in the face of difficulty. The word carries the idea of a prolonged struggle that demands courage, discipline, and endurance until the end.
G0118.origine: The Greek word comes from the root ἆθλος (athos), which denotes "struggle" or "combat" in the context of games and war. It is a sporting term that evokes the ancient athlete engaged in an official competition. The family of words includes the athlete himself and the crown that rewards his victory.
G0118.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 2:5. Paul uses it to encourage Timothy to live the Christian life like an athlete who fights loyally. The image is that of a regulated sports competition, where victory belongs only to those who respect the rules. This passage likens the Christian commitment to a sports struggle where discipline and obedience are essential to obtain the reward.
G0118.portee: This word invites the Christian to see his faith as a noble and regulated struggle, not chaotic or disorganized. It teaches that perseverance in faith is not a matter of brute strength, but of respecting the principles and order established by God. It is an encouragement to pursue with courage and discipline, knowing that the crown of victory is reserved only for those who fight "according to the rules."

sens: Confrontation between athletes during games or physical trials
General struggle or conflict, opposition
Difficult trial to endure or overcome
G0119.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the athletic combat of athletes, the test of strength or technique they deliver during games. This is the physical and concrete sense of the word, forged in the world of ancient competitions.
2. It then extends to any conflict or opposition, any struggle, not just physical: it is the image of a fight in a broad sense.
3. In the New Testament, it takes on a figurative sense to designate a difficult trial, a suffering that the Christian must endure and overcome with perseverance. In Hebrews 10:32, the early Christians "endured a great struggle amidst sufferings": they faced trials, persecutions, like one confronts an adversary.
G0119.origine: The word comes from the root ἀθλέω (athleuō) which means "to fight like an athlete" or "to struggle." It is itself linked to ἄθλος (athlos), "the struggle" or "the trial," which evokes effort and hardship. The starting image is thus that of athletic combat, which has enriched the figurative sense of struggle against adversity and suffering.
G0119.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 10:32. There it designates the sufferings and persecutions that the first readers of this letter endured after their conversion. The author encourages them by reminding them that they have already "endured a great struggle": he borrows the image of the athlete facing trials to show that Christian trials are a form of combat to be fought with courage and tenacity, like an athlete.
G0119.portee: This word reminds the Christian that the trials of faith are not accidents or injustices, but challenges to be met, just as an athlete faces his trials. It invites one to consider sufferings with dignity and combativeness, not with passive resignation. The Christian life is also a struggle, but a struggle that has meaning and prepares for victory.

sens: Lose confidence and energy in the face of difficulties
Lose the desire to continue, become demoralized
Be discouraged in heart and spirit
G0120.detail:
1. The Greek verb literally means "to be without heart": it is to lose courage and moral strength in the face of a difficult or oppressive situation. The image evokes someone whose heart has been emptied of determination. In Colossians 3:21, Paul exhorts fathers not to provoke their children "lest they become discouraged" — meaning that overly harsh authority can demoralize them and paralyze their confidence.
2. The word describes the state of a person who loses the desire to act, to progress, or to make an effort. A child who is overly criticized or mistreated becomes discouraged: he gives up, he renounces. It is the opposite of the courage and perseverance that faith demands.
G0120.origine: The word comes from the negative root "a-" (without) joined to "thymos," which means heart, spirit, passion. Literally: "without heart." In Hebrew, the verb "chara" (to blaze, to become angry) or expressions of similar meaning translated this idea of moral loss and demoralization. This image of the "heart" is common in the Bible to designate the seat of will and courage.
G0120.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Colossians 3:21. Paul uses it in his recommendation to fathers: not to "discourage" their children through excessive strictness or constant irritation. It is a call to educational kindness. The context shows that this verb concerns psychological and moral state: losing confidence, becoming demoralized, renouncing. It is a serious risk for children in formation, who need encouragement.
G0120.portee: This word reminds Christians — and particularly those in authority — that their words and actions have a tremendous weight on the morale and confidence of others. To discourage someone is to take away their courage to follow Christ and to grow. Conversely, encouraging is a major pastoral responsibility. The passage invites exercising authority with wisdom and love, without hardening hearts.

sens: Who has not committed the fault or crime of which he is accused
Who does not deserve the punishment inflicted upon him
Who is pure, free from guilt
G0121.detail:
1. The word designates someone who has not committed the reprehensible act for which he is held responsible. Judas acknowledges that Jesus is "innocent" of the bloodshed (Matthew 27:4): Jesus has done nothing that justifies his condemnation to death.
2. It is also one who does not deserve the punishment imposed upon him. When Pilate washes his hands, he declares: "I am innocent of the blood of this just man" (Matthew 27:24) — he asserts that he bears no responsibility for this execution.
3. More broadly, the word expresses the absence of guilt: innocence as moral purity and absence of fault.
G0121.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that evokes the absence of penalty or punishment. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates verbs meaning "to be pure" or "to be declared innocent." Innocence is not naivety, but the clarity of conscience of a person who has nothing to reproach themselves for.
G0121.emploi: This word appears twice in the New Testament, both times in Matthew during the trial of Jesus. Judas uses it to acknowledge that Jesus is innocent, while he has just betrayed him. Pilate uses it to decline his responsibility in the death of Jesus. In both cases, it is about affirming the absence of guilt before an imminent execution. The tragic irony lies in the fact that those who pronounce the word recognize Jesus' innocence but cannot or will not protect it.
G0121.portee: This word confronts us with the reality of Jesus' innocence in the face of his condemnation. It invites us to reflect on justice: Jesus dies innocent, which gives his death a profound dimension — not as punishment for a personal fault, but as a voluntary offering for our faults. For the believer, Christ's innocence at the time of his Passion is the foundation of faith in his redemptive sacrifice.

sens: Belonging to or derived from the goat
G0122.detail: 1. An adjective that describes what is related to the goat or comes from it. In Hebrews 11:37, the Apostle Paul lists the sufferings endured by the faithful of the Old Testament: some, stripped and persecuted, wrapped themselves in goat skins to protect themselves from the cold and misery. This image evokes rudimentary clothing, coarse fabrics, symbols of poverty and abandonment.
G0122.origine: The word comes from the Greek αἶξ (aix), which means "goat." The goat, an easy-to-raise and useful animal (milk, meat, skins), has been a part of the economy of Middle Eastern peoples since ancient times. In Hebrew, עֵז (ez) also refers to the goat, and the Greek word is close in meaning and etymology.
G0122.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:37. Paul enumerates the trials of the believers of the Old Testament—stoning, saws, sword, flight—and mentions among these signs of destitution the goat skins that some wore, alongside the skins of sheep. The context emphasizes the poverty and suffering endured for faith.
G0122.portee: This mention of goat skins reminds the Christian reader that faithfulness to God spans history through men and women who have lost everything, reduced to total destitution. It honors those who, lacking better, settled for the bare necessities to persevere in faith. It is an invitation not to measure faithfulness by the comfort of the present.

sens: The edge of the sea, the beach where water meets land
The place where one stops when coming from the sea or before departing by boat
G0123.detail:
1. The shore is the edge of the sea, the strip of land and sand that borders the water. It is the place where the waves arrive and where one can walk between the water and the dry land. In Matthew 13:2, a large crowd gathers on the shore of the lake to listen to Jesus, who is about to get into a boat; it is a place of passage and meeting between land and water.
2. The shore is also the point of departure or arrival for all those traveling by boat. In Acts 21:5, the disciples accompany Paul to the shore and pray with him before his departure; in Acts 27:39-40, the shipwrecked sailors look for a shore to direct the ship to save it. It is the point of contact between two worlds: that of dry land and that of the sea.
G0123.origine: The Greek word aigialos comes from a root that evokes the idea of limit or edge. It literally designates the boundary between two elements: land and sea. In Hebrew, equivalent words like chof (חוֹף) have the same meaning in the Old Testament.
G0123.emploi: The word "shore" appears six times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Acts. It is used in a concrete and geographical sense: Matthew uses it to describe the context of Jesus' teachings by the lake (13:2, 13:48); John mentions it when Jesus appears on the shore after his resurrection (21:4); Luke (Acts) uses it to situate important moments: farewells before a journey (21:5) or the desperate search for a place to run aground a ship (27:39-40). It is always a precise geographical location, never figurative.
G0123.portee: The shore in the Bible is often the meeting place between Jesus and his disciples, or between the apostle and his companions. It is a space of transition: one prays before departing, listens to the Word, appears resurrected. For the Christian reader, the shore reminds us that faith is lived in concrete places and moments, not in the abstract: it requires stopping, listening, and praying together before moving forward.

sens: Belonging to Egypt, its people or its civilization
An inhabitant of Egypt
A man from Egypt (as opposed to a Hebrew or a Greek)
G0124.detail:
1. This word designates anything that comes from Egypt or is of Egyptian origin. In Acts 7:22, Moses "was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians," meaning he received all the education, knowledge, and culture that the Egyptians could offer at the royal palace.
2. The word also refers to a man from Egypt. In Acts 7:24, Moses "struck the Egyptian"—an Egyptian man who was mistreating a Hebrew. Similarly, in Acts 21:38, the Roman tribune asks Paul if he is "that Egyptian" who had led a revolt.
3. In a religious and biblical context, "Egyptian" designates one who does not know God—the unbeliever. Hebrews 11:29 recounts that the Egyptians who attempted to cross the Red Sea "were drowned," while the Hebrews, by faith, crossed it safely. It is the mark of one who opposes God's plan.
G0124.origine: This word comes from the Greek name for Egypt, Aiguptos (Αἲγυπτος), which itself corresponds to an ancient Egyptian word. The adjective is formed simply by adding a standard ending to the noun, which makes it a qualifier. This is how adjectives are regularly formed in Greek: from the name of a country, one derives the adjective "inhabitant of that country" or "belonging to that country."
G0124.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the New Testament, concentrated in two passages: the preaching of Stephen in Acts 7 and a brief mention in Acts 21. In Stephen's speech, "Egyptian" evokes Moses' worldly education (7:22) and the violence between Hebrews and Egyptians at the time of Moses (7:24 and 7:28). In Acts 21:38, the word designates a revolutionary leader. Finally, in Hebrews 11:29, the Egyptians embody unbelief and opposition to God. The meaning thus nuances from cultural identity to the status of enemy of the faith.
G0124.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of God's history with his people. The Egyptians are never simply a historical nation: they represent the power of the world, unbelief, and hostility toward God. Seeing the Egyptians "drowned" in the Red Sea (Hebrews 11:29) invites the believer to trust in God rather than the forces of the world.

sens: Country in North Africa, ancient kingdom located along the Nile
Place of refuge and exile for the people of Israel
Power that oppresses and enslaves the people of God
Biblical symbol of hostility towards God and His will
G0125.detail:
1. Egypt is the great country of Africa that stretches along the Nile: it is an important power of the ancient world, with its king the Pharaoh and its governors. In the Gospels, Joseph flees there with the child Jesus to escape death, on the order of an angel (Matthew 2:13).
2. Egypt is the country where Israel stayed for a long time, where Jacob and his sons went down, and where the people had to serve in slavery (Acts 7:15). It was from this country that God brought His people out with power, through Moses, for forty years in the desert (Acts 7:36).
3. The word evokes oppression and enslavement: Israel experienced servitude and forced labor there, and it is from this condition of slavery that God saved them. This explains why Egypt symbolizes the slavery of sin in biblical theology.
4. In Revelation (11:8), Jerusalem itself is called "Egypt" to show that it has become hostile to God, rejecting the cross of Christ: the word then becomes a spiritual image of rebellion against God.
G0125.origine: The Greek name "Aiguptos" comes from the ancient Egyptian name of the country. The Greek text of the New Testament uses this name to refer to both the geographical country and the nation. When we say "the land of Egypt" or "the country of Egypt," we emphasize the importance of this territory as a world power at the time of the Old Testament.
G0125.emploi: The word "Egypt" appears about 23 times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts (where Stephen recounts the history of Israel) and in the epistles. It primarily designates the geographical country: a place of refuge for the child Jesus (Matthew 2), the land of servitude for the people of Israel (Acts 7:9-40). Then, in Revelation 11:8, Jerusalem is figuratively called "Egypt" because it has rejected Christ — Egypt then becomes a symbol of rebellion against God. In all cases, the word reminds the Church that God saves those who cry out to Him from their servitude.
G0125.portee: Egypt shows us that God does not leave His people in servitude: He brings them out by a manifest power. For the Christian, this journey reminds us that deliverance from sin comes from God alone. Moreover, the fate of Jerusalem called "Egypt" warns us: rejecting Christ means placing oneself under the yoke of spiritual oppression. The name Egypt in the Bible always speaks of salvation or judgment.

sens: That lasts forever, without beginning or end
That exists independently of time
That remains unchanged through the ages
G0126.detail:
1. The word designates what is eternal in the absolute sense: having no beginning or end, lasting perpetually. In Romans 1:20, the eternal power of God refers to His nature that completely transcends time and knows neither birth nor death.

2. It is also what remains unchanged and permanent, beyond the flow of human generations. In Jude 1:6, the angels are chained "eternally": this bond will never be broken, it persists in eternity.

3. The word applies to what belongs to the divine order, timeless and absolute, in contrast to what is temporal and transient. It is divine eternity itself, that of God and His attributes.
G0126.origine: The word comes from the Greek root meaning "always" (ἀεί). It is very close to the word αἰώνιος (aïonios), which also means "eternal," but aidios emphasizes the absolute and timeless aspect, while aïonios can also refer to very long periods of ages. In ancient Greek texts, this distinction gradually fades, and the two words end up being used interchangeably.
G0126.emploi: The word aidios appears only twice in the New Testament. In Romans 1:20, Paul uses it to qualify the power of God that everyone can perceive in creation: it is the divine attribute par excellence, showing that God totally transcends time. In Jude 1:6, he describes the chains that hold the rebellious angels: this word emphasizes that their punishment will have no end, that it pertains to the eternal order of God. In both cases, the word stresses absolute permanence and timelessness.
G0126.portee: This word reminds us that God is not subject to time as we are. By seeing it qualify the power of God and eternal judgment, the reader is invited to recognize the infinite greatness of God and the reality of divine judgment that will never pass away. This anchors faith in a reality that transcends our temporal limits.

sens: feeling of restraint and reserve in the face of what might be shameful or inappropriate
purity, discretion in appearance and clothing
respectful fear of displeasing or violating propriety
G0127.detail:
1. Modesty is primarily an inner feeling: it is the ability to feel shame or discomfort in the presence of what is indecent or transgresses propriety. It is a sensitivity to honor, a fear of doing something shameful. In 1 Timothy 2:9, Paul advises women to adorn themselves "with modesty and propriety": they should wear decent clothing, with the inner awareness that they should not attract attention through lavish adornments.
2. By extension, this feeling is concretely expressed in conduct and appearance: modesty then becomes a visible restraint, a discretion in the way one dresses, behaves in public. It is refusing ostentation and extravagance to maintain a simple and reserved dignity.
3. More broadly, it is also a respectful fear of offending, causing scandal, or displeasing others — a consciousness of the gaze of others tempered by the concern to remain within the limits of what is proper.
G0127.origine: The word comes from a Greek root related to the idea of fear and respect. The starting image is that of a sensitivity to shame, a capacity to blush or feel embarrassment. This natural sense of modesty distinguishes the word αἰδώς from αἰσχύνη (shame, dishonor), which rather designates the state of shame itself rather than the feeling of restraint that prevents it. It is the difference between having a moral conscience that restrains you (modesty) and experiencing shame for a fault committed.
G0127.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 2:9. Paul writes this in the context of practical recommendations to the women of the Christian community: they should dress decently, with modesty and propriety, rather than seeking to shine through costly adornments (gold, pearls, elaborate hairstyles, sumptuous clothes). Paul does not condemn adornment in itself, but he calls for conscious restraint and a hierarchy of values: the true beauty of a woman should come from her piety and character, not from her wealth. This word reflects the values of dignity and propriety that characterize the early Christian ethos.
G0127.portee: For the Christian, this word invites reflection on the relationship between outward appearance and inner life. Modesty is not a matter of rigid dress codes, but the expression of an attitude: one that says "what truly matters in me is what I am in God, not what I possess or display." It is a virtue that protects both personal honor and respect for others, an antidote to vanity and pride that can corrupt even the Christian life.

sens: inhabitant de l'Éthiopie, ancien royaume africain situé au sud de l'Égypte
G0128.detail: 1. The word refers to a man from Ethiopia, the ancient African kingdom located in the interior of East Africa, south of Egypt. In Acts 8:27, this Ethiopian is a powerful eunuch, minister of the queen, which shows that Ethiopians at that time played an important role in Mediterranean and Near Eastern kingdoms.
G0128.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: *aïthô* (to burn) and *ops* (face, look). It literally means "one who has a burned face" or "with a darkened face," as the Greeks referred to the dark-skinned peoples from south of the Nile. This same people was called in Hebrew *Kouch* or *Cush*, a term that also appears in the Old Testament to designate the region south of Egypt.
G0128.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 8:27, where Luke mentions it to describe a high-ranking official. This Ethiopian was a eunuch and served the queen of Ethiopia as her treasurer. The account shows that he was devout enough to travel to Jerusalem to worship God at the temple, and it is on his way back that Philip meets him and shares the Gospel. This brief mention reveals that the Good News was already spreading to distant regions and to high-ranking individuals.
G0128.portee: This passage reminds us that the Gospel was not intended only for the Jews of Jerusalem or the Greco-Roman Mediterranean, but that it was gradually extending to the farthest lands. The conversion of this Ethiopian symbolizes universal access to salvation in Christ, beyond national, ethnic, and social boundaries.

sens: Red liquid that circulates in the veins and arteries of living beings
Lineage, family origin, kinship ties
Red color resembling blood
Violent death or murder, especially in phrases of responsibility
Animal sacrifice whose blood was shed for the atonement of sins
Sacrifice of Jesus Christ offered for the forgiveness of humanity's sins
G0129G.detail:
1. Blood in the literal sense of the living body: this vital liquid that flows from a wound. Luke 8:44 speaks of the woman with a hemorrhage who has been bleeding for twelve years; John 19:34 describes the blood that flowed from the side of crucified Jesus.
2. Descent and kinship: "flesh and blood" (Matthew 16:17) refers to human nature linked to family heredity. This means that Simon did not receive the revelation from his own fleshly family, but from God alone.
3. The red color of blood: Revelation 6:12 speaks of cosmic phenomena where the moon becomes like blood, an image of calamity.
4. Murder and guilt: "the blood of Abel" (Luke 11:51) means the murder committed; "to demand account of the blood" means to seek justice for this murder. Matthew 27:25 shows the crowd accepting "his blood upon us."
5. The atoning sacrifice in the Temple: Hebrews 9:22 explains that without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness, for the blood shed on the altar made atonement for sins.
6. The sacrifice of Christ: the blood of Jesus shed on the cross is the ultimate offering that takes away sins. 1 John 1:7 affirms that this blood cleanses us from all sin; 1 Peter 1:19 presents it as the price of our redemption.
G0129G.origine: The Greek word ahima (blood) translates the Hebrew dam, which primarily designates the vital liquid of life. The Bible makes blood much more than a simple substance: it is the seat of life itself, for "the life of the flesh is in the blood" (Leviticus 17:11). From the Old Testament, the shed blood cries out to God (Genesis 4:10), and sacrificial blood purifies (Leviticus 17:11). The New Testament takes up this language to describe both the bloody death of Jesus and its incomparable redemptive value.
G0129G.emploi: The word appears about 90 times in the New Testament, especially in the Passion narratives and in the exegetical epistles of salvation. Matthew, Mark, and Luke report the institution of the Last Supper with the "blood of the covenant shed for the forgiveness of sins" (Matthew 26:28). The epistle to the Hebrews elaborates (9-10) on how the sacrifice of Jesus replaces the old system of sacrifices: his blood is more effective than that of bulls and goats. Paul, in Romans 3:25 and 5:9, affirms that we are justified by this blood and redeemed from the wrath of God. John, in his Revelation, uses blood to emphasize both redemption (5:9: "redeemed for God by your blood") and judgment (6:10: the blood of the martyrs crying out for vengeance). The expression "flesh and blood" describes the weak and mortal human nature, opposed to God (Ephesians 6:12).
G0129G.portee: The blood of Jesus is at the heart of the evangelical message: it reminds the believer that his salvation has a real price, paid at the cross, and that it is not obtained by his own efforts. Meditating on the blood of the Covenant invites gratitude and worship. It also teaches us that our filiation does not depend on our natural parents, but on our attachment to Christ: only the blood of Jesus cleanses us and reconciles us with God.

sens: The red liquid that circulates in the veins and arteries
Violent death, the shedding of blood
Human nature, mortal flesh, family origin
The blood shed in sacrifice for the atonement of sins
G0129H.detail:
1. Blood is the vital liquid that flows in the bodies of living creatures. This is the ordinary meaning of the word in the Bible, found in accounts of the sick or miracles: the woman suffering from a hemorrhage (Mark 5:25) is healed by the power of Jesus.

2. Blood also refers to murder and violence – unjustly shed death. When Jesus reproaches the religious leaders for having shed the "blood" of the prophets (Matthew 23:35), he speaks of crime, of murder. The "field of blood" (Acts 1:19) bears this grim name because Judas met a violent death there.

3. "Flesh and blood" (Matthew 16:17) means our fragile and mortal human nature, which can do nothing by itself before God. It is also what binds a family: having the same blood means being of the same origin, of the same clan.

4. In the sacrifices of the Old Testament and especially in Jesus Christ, blood represents life offered for atonement – the forgiveness of sins. The blood of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:16) is what seals the new covenant between God and his people.
G0129H.origine: The Greek word αἷμα comes from a very ancient root designating the vital liquid of creatures. It translates the Hebrew דָּם (dam) in the Greek Bible of the Old Testament. In both Hebrew and Greek, blood is intimately linked to life itself: "The life of the flesh is in the blood" (Leviticus 17:11). The word always retains this density: it never designates a simple substance, but life, death, covenant, moral responsibility.
G0129H.emploi: The word appears mainly in two contexts: first, the Passion narrative, where the blood of Christ flowing at the cross becomes the heart of Christian salvation (Hebrews 9-10 elaborates on this theme). Then, Acts and Revelation use "blood" to speak of murder and guilt – notably the "field of blood" (Acts 1:19) which recalls Judas's betrayal. In the Epistles, "flesh and blood" (Ephesians 6:12) denotes our limited human condition in the face of spiritual powers. Finally, the New Testament takes up the sacrificial imagery of the Old: the shed blood purifies and establishes the covenant with God.
G0129H.portee: The blood of Christ is not a historical detail, but the very foundation of Christian forgiveness. Understanding that Jesus shed his blood "for the remission of sins" (Matthew 26:28) transforms faith: it is not an abstract doctrine, but the concrete act of love that reconciles the sinner with God. Meditating on the blood of Christ is entering into gratitude for the price of our redemption.

sens: Spilling of blood, poured out of the veins
Ritual sacrifice where blood is poured out for purification or forgiveness
Fulfillment of the Law through bloody sacrifice
G0130.detail:
1. The word literally refers to blood that flows out, poured out of the body. It is the image of blood shed, as in a fatal wound or a sacrifice where blood is poured on the altar.
2. In the context of Israelite worship, bloodshed is the central act of sacrifice: the animal is killed and its blood is poured out according to the prescriptions of the Law. It is through this poured-out blood that purification and forgiveness become possible (Hebrews 9:22).
3. The Apostle Paul uses this word to say that without this ritual shedding of blood, no forgiveness exists; it is the heart of what the Law required to remove sin.
G0130.origine: The Greek word is composed of two roots: "haima" (blood) and "ekcheô" (to pour out, to shed). The image is that of blood flowing outward. This compound exists in both classical and biblical Greek to describe the pouring out of blood in sacrifices or murder. It translates the Hebrew idea of shed blood, central to all purification according to the Mosaic Law.
G0130.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 9:22, in a crucial passage about sacrifice and forgiveness. The author of the epistle establishes that the Law itself requires the shedding of blood for the remission of sins. Paul or the author uses it to show that without the shedding of blood, there is no forgiveness according to the old order. It refers to the sacrificial system of the temple and the fulfillment of these sacrifices in Christ.
G0130.portee: This word opens to Christians the understanding of the heart of the Old Testament: why so many bloody sacrifices? Because the Law itself ties the forgiveness of sins to the shedding of blood. This illuminates the value of Christ's sacrifice, His blood shed on the cross as the perfect and definitive fulfillment of all these ancient figures. It is also a call to take seriously the reality of sin and the price of its redemption.

sens: To suffer from a continuous and abundant loss of blood
To be afflicted with a chronic hemorrhage
G0131.detail:
1. The word literally describes a loss of blood that flows from the body continuously and involuntarily. This is the case of the woman whom Jesus meets in Matthew 9:20, who had suffered for twelve years from a constant flow of blood: she was exhausted, weakened, and rendered unclean according to the law of Moses.

2. In a broader sense, it refers to a chronic and debilitating illness, a condition that deprives the person of strength, dignity, and social status — which is why this woman approaches Jesus secretly, hoping for healing.
G0131.origine: The word comes from the combination of two Greek roots: "aima" (αἷμα), which means blood, and "rhoē" (ῥέω), which means to flow or to run. The image is thus that of blood flowing out of the body. In Hebrew, the condition is designated by the word "dāwāh," which also evokes this loss of bodily fluid.
G0131.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Matthew 9:20, where it describes the condition of a woman suffering from a hemorrhage for twelve years. She came to touch the hem of Jesus' garment, certain that this contact would heal her. It is a medical and personal detail that reveals the depth of her suffering and despair, as well as her boldness and faith.
G0131.portee: This story reminds Christians that Jesus welcomes and heals those who suffer in isolation and humiliation — not with judgment, but with compassion. The woman with the hemorrhage represents all those who feel excluded or unclean, and who find in Jesus physical and spiritual restoration.

sens: Paralyzed man in Lydda, healed by Peter
G0132.detail: Aeneas is a man living in Lydda (a city in Judea) at the time of the apostles. He had been lying on a bed for eight years, completely paralyzed. Peter meets him and, in the name of Jesus Christ, heals him instantly: Aeneas gets up and makes his bed (Acts 9:33-34). This miracle becomes a powerful sign that leads many inhabitants of Lydda and the coastal region to believe in the Lord.
G0132.origine: Aeneas is a common Greek name in antiquity. The name literally means "praised" or "worthy of praise," but in the biblical context, it simply refers to a man living in Judea in the first century. The Bible does not provide any information about his life before his paralysis or anything after his healing.
G0132.emploi: Aeneas appears only twice in the Bible, both in Acts 9:33-34. It is in the context of Peter's ministry after Pentecost. His story illustrates the power of Jesus Christ who heals the sick through the apostles, even those who have been paralyzed for a long time. This miraculous healing has a significant spiritual impact throughout the region.
G0132.portee: The story of Aeneas shows us that Jesus Christ can heal even the most desperate cases — an eight-year paralysis. It also teaches us that the miracles of the apostles were never ends in themselves, but signs that brought people to faith. For the believer, the account of Aeneas is an invitation to believe that God can intervene in our most difficult situations.

sens: Expression of gratitude and admiration directed to God
Act of confessing the name and works of God through words
Spiritual sacrifice or offering presented to God
G0133.detail:
1. Praise is the expression of our gratitude and admiration towards God. It is a movement of the heart that translates into words to acknowledge who God is and what He has done. In Hebrews 13:15, the apostle exhorts us to offer a "sacrifice of praise," which shows that praising God is a voluntary and precious act.
2. Praise consists of confessing the name of God with our lips, that is, publicly proclaiming who He is and recognizing His authority. When we praise God, we affirm His greatness and goodness. It is not mere flattery: it is testifying to the truth of who He is.
3. In biblical language, praise is a sacrifice offered to God — not an animal or an object, but an offering of words. Hebrews 13:15 speaks of the "fruit of lips that confess His name": this refers to the verbal confession of God that becomes a spiritual offering pleasing to God, more precious than the material sacrifices of the Old Testament.
G0133.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "aineô" which means "to praise" or "to celebrate." In the Greek of the Old Testament, this word primarily translates the Hebrew "todah" (thanksgiving, confession) and "tehillah" (hymn, song of praise). Biblical praise is not vague or ambiguous: it is always tied to a specific recognition of who God is and what He has accomplished. It is a word that springs from knowledge and the heart.
G0133.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 13:15. It is used to describe the "sacrifice of praise" that Christians should continually offer to God through Jesus Christ. It is a teaching on prayer and Christian worship: while the Old Testament prescribed animal sacrifices (like the one described in Leviticus 7:12), the New Testament affirms that the true sacrifice offered to God is verbal praise, the confessing expression of our faith. This sacrifice is perpetual ("continually") and accessible to every believer.
G0133.portee: Praise reminds us that our relationship with God is not a matter of religious performance or material expenditure, but of authentic words and a confessing heart. By calling praise a "sacrifice," the Bible shows us that it costs something: it requires humility, vulnerability, and obedience of the heart. For the Christian, continually offering to God a sacrifice of praise is the very heart of worship and the life of prayer.

sens: To express admiration and gratitude towards someone, particularly towards God
To proclaim the greatness and merits of someone
To celebrate through words or songs
To give glory and honor
G0134.detail:
1. To praise is to express aloud one's admiration and gratitude towards God for His wonderful acts. It is to acknowledge His greatness through words. The shepherds, after seeing the newborn Jesus, returned "glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen" (Luke 2:20): their hearts overflowed with gratitude and they spoke about it.
2. To praise also means to publicly proclaim God's greatness, to make it known to others. In Jerusalem, the disciples began to "praise God loudly for all the miracles they had seen" (Luke 19:37): it was not a private word, but an audible declaration before all the people.
3. It is to celebrate God through songs and words, as the angels did: "suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising God" (Luke 2:13). This praise could take the form of song or solemn prayer.
4. Finally, to praise is to give glory and honor to God, to treat Him as He deserves, to give Him the foremost place in the heart and on the lips. It is an act of joyful submission to the Lord.
G0134.origine: The Greek verb αἰνέω comes from the noun αἶνος, which means "praise" or "commendation." It is a poetic and literary word, rarer in classical Greek, but very common in the New Testament and the Greek Bible. It generally translates the Hebrew הִלֵּל (hilel, "to praise"), which shares the same root. The word thus expresses a verbal acknowledgment, a word that rises to God or magnifies Him before men.
G0134.emploi: The verb αἰνέω appears nine times in the New Testament (Segond 1910 translation), almost exclusively in the Gospels of Luke and Acts, at moments when joy and thanksgiving burst forth. The shepherds praise God after the birth of Jesus (Luke 2:20), the disciples praise after the healing of the paralytic (Acts 3:8–9) and during the triumphal entry into Jerusalem (Luke 19:37). It is also found in Jerusalem after Pentecost (Acts 2:47), and in Revelation when the living and the dead praise God (Revelation 19:5). The context is always one of joy, deliverance, and acknowledgment of a divine intervention. The word can be constructed with the accusative ("to praise God," τὸν θεόν) or the dative ("to praise to God," τῷ θεῷ).
G0134.portee: Praising God is not a luxury or a politeness: it is the natural reaction of a healed heart, of a saved sinner, of a witness to a miracle. It is also a public act: one praises "loudly" and "continuously," meaning that praise does not remain locked inside; it bursts forth and persists. For the Christian, to praise is a mark of true conversion and acknowledgment towards God; it is also a word that strengthens faith and builds up others.

sens: An obscure word, a question difficult to understand
A discourse wrapped in mystery, where the meaning does not appear clearly
