Secondly, "unclean spirits" saturate the synoptic Gospels: Jesus constantly encounters them, casts them out, and recognizes their demonic nature. Thirdly, Paul uses the word morally to describe the state of the human heart corrupted by sin or idolatry (Ephesians 5:5; 2 Corinthians 6:17). The notion of impurity is thus progressively internalized: it moves from the external rules of the law to the internal reality of demonic possession and moral corruption.
G0169.portee: For the believer, understanding this notion of impurity invites recognition that sin contaminates us and separates us from God far more than food or ritual practices do. Paul's call in 2 Corinthians 6:17 to "separate" from what is impure becomes a call to personal holiness: to examine not only our actions but our thoughts and desires. Finally, the constant mention of "unclean spirits" in the Gospels affirms that Jesus has the power to free those who are under the dominion of evil, a promise of deliverance and spiritual purification offered to anyone who turns to him.

sens: not having the right moment to act
not having the favorable possibility to do something
G0170.detail:
1. This verb expresses the absence of a favorable occasion, a suitable moment to accomplish an action. It is the opposite of having a good opportunity: one would like to do something, but the time has not come or the circumstances do not allow it. In Philippians 4:10, Paul says of the Philippians: "you were thinking well, but the opportunity was lacking" — they desired to show him their affection but had not had the chance to do so until then.
2. The word emphasizes an involuntary deprivation: it is not that one does not want to, but that one cannot, due to a lack of favorable circumstances. It is a painful situation where goodwill exists, but external conditions do not lend themselves to it.
G0170.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective ἄκαιρος ("inopportune, out of season"), formed by the negation ἀ- and the word καιρός ("opportune moment, favorable occasion"). The verb ἀκαιρέω literally means "to be without occasion." Its antonym is εὐκαιρέω ("to have a good occasion"). This family of words shows the importance that the biblical mentality attributes to the notion of the right time, the moment when God allows an action to bear fruit.
G0170.emploi: This Greek verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Philippians 4:10. Paul thanks the Church of Philippi for its constant support and expressions of affection. He acknowledges that the Philippians sincerely loved him and thought of him, but that a long period had passed without them having the opportunity to express this to him concretely. The context shows that there is no reproach here: Paul understands that the lack of opportunity, not a lack of love, explained the silence. It is a word of encouragement and mutual understanding in the communion of the Church.
G0170.portee: This word reminds us that there is a crucial difference between lacking will and lacking opportunity. When someone we love does not reach out to us, we may too quickly assume that they have forgotten us; the text teaches us to also consider the possibility that they simply lack opportunity. It is a word of patience and grace in our fraternal relationships: recognizing this difference helps to preserve communion and love despite delays.

sens: At the wrong time, contrary to what circumstances allow
In an untimely or inappropriate manner
Against the favorable moment or occasion
G0171.detail:
1. The word describes an action undertaken at the wrong time, when circumstances do not lend themselves to it. It is the opposite of doing something "wisely" or "in a timely manner." In 2 Timothy 4:2, Paul asks Pastor Timothy to preach the Word "in every occasion, favorable or not": this means that the proclamation of the Gospel must continue even when the moment seems unpropitious.
2. The word implies a certain clumsiness or lack of discernment regarding the appropriate moment. It is not just about doing something at a bad time, but doing it without regard for the circumstances that should guide our action.
3. In a broader sense, the adverb characterizes any intervention that has not waited for the favorable moment, which does not take into account the opportunity.
G0171.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "ἀ-" (which negates or reverses) and the adjective "καῖρος" (kairos, opportune moment, favorable occasion). It literally means "not opportune" or "against the kairos." Biblical Greek uses this kairos to designate the decisive moment, the right time when action becomes appropriate. Its Greek opposite, "εὐκαίρως" (eukairos), means precisely "on every occasion, favorably."
G0171.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in 2 Timothy 4:2. Paul exhorts Timothy to preach "in every occasion, favorable or not." It is a call to pastoral perseverance: the preacher should not wait for the ideal moment to announce the Word, but should be ready to do so even when there is little interest, when the audience is hostile, or when circumstances seem unfavorable. The adverb emphasizes the tenacity required of the minister of the Word.
G0171.portee: This word reminds the believer that obedience to God does not depend on external circumstances. For a pastor or a simple Christian called to witness, this means not waiting for the "perfect" moment to speak of their faith. True spiritual courage consists in moving forward faithfully, even "inopportunely" according to the world, knowing that God places his opportunities.

sens: Who is without guile, malice, and ignorance of wickedness
Who is without guilt, pure of all reproach
Exempt from malice or duplicity
G0172.detail:
1. The word describes a person who is naive, without calculation or ulterior motives. They are unaware of cunning and deception — which is why seducers target the "simple" in Romans 16:18, people easily deceived by "smooth and flattering words."
2. It also denotes moral innocence: the one who is "simple" is pure, without guilt, without blemish. This is the innocence of the high priest described in Hebrews 7:26, who is "innocent" — without malice or guilt — and "without blemish."
3. Beyond naivety, the word evokes a purity of intention: one who does not harbor the seed of evil, who does not act out of calculation or duplicity.
G0172.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "not containing evil" (the privative prefix α- "without" and κάκη "malice"). In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it translates Hebrew words like תָּם (tam, "whole, upright") and פְּתִי (pethi, "naive"), which evoke candor and integrity. The Greek word retains this dual shade: moral innocence and absence of cunning.
G0172.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, in two distinct contexts. In Romans 16:18, Paul warns against those who deceive the "simple" with flattering words — this is naive innocence, vulnerability to lies. In Hebrews 7:26, the same word describes the ideal high priest, innocent of all guilt and malice — this is moral innocence and purity of heart. In both cases, it is an absence: absence of cunning in the naive, absence of malice in the perfect priest.
G0172.portee: This word reminds us that simplicity is not a weakness: it can be vulnerability (we must be wary of those who exploit the simple), but it is also a virtue when it expresses purity of heart and absence of duplicity. Jesus himself invites us to become "wise as serpents and innocent as doves" to enter the kingdom.

sens: Thorny plant, bush covered with thorns
Symbol of what hurts, wounds, or destroys
What chokes the Word of God in the heart
Instrument of mockery and suffering
G0173.detail:
1. A thorn is a plant covered with sharp thorns, often a wild bush or thistle that grows in uncultivated land. Jesus uses it to show that one cannot gather grapes from thorns, as in Matthew 7:16: a bad plant produces only bad fruit.
2. The thorn symbolizes what causes suffering, what pricks and wounds. It is the image of evil and destruction: in the parable of the sower (Matthew 13:7), the thorns that grow choke the sown grain and prevent it from growing.
3. In the human heart, thorns represent the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches that choke the Word of God and make it unfruitful in us (Matthew 13:22) — which diverts us from following God.
4. At the Passion, Jesus suffers a crown of thorns placed on his head (Matthew 27:29 and John 19:2): the thorns become the instrument of mockery, humiliation, and suffering of the Son of God.
G0173.origine: The Greek word ἄκανθα comes from a root meaning "point" or "thorn." It translates the Hebrew קוֹץ (qôtz), the word used in the Old Testament to refer to thorns and thistles that cover abandoned or cursed land. This image of prickliness, of what wounds, is very ancient in human imagination.
G0173.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the New Testament, always in the plural. It is mainly concentrated in the Gospels: in Matthew and Mark in the parable of the sower (where thorns symbolize obstacles to the fruit of the Word), in Luke in similar contexts, and in John at the time of the Passion. Hebrews 6:8 uses it to speak of land that produces only thorns and thistles, that is, a barren life. From passage to passage, the thorn oscillates between the concrete (a plant that pricks) and the figurative (what destroys spiritual fruit, what symbolizes the suffering of Christ).
G0173.portee: The word "thorn" teaches the believer two essential things: first, that the Word of God can be choked in us by the cares and riches of the world (Matthew 13:22), which invites us to guard our hearts; secondly, that Jesus wore a crown of thorns for us, reconciling the thorn (symbol of curse since Genesis) with our salvation. The thorn thus reminds us of the price of our redemption and the reality of Christ's suffering.

sens: Made of thorns or consisting of thorns
Having the nature or appearance of a thorn
G0174.detail:
1. The word literally designates what is composed of thorns or made from thorns. In the two passages of the New Testament, it qualifies the crown that the Roman soldiers wove and placed on Jesus' head before his crucifixion (Mark 15:17; John 19:5): a crown made of thorny branches, an instrument of torture and mockery.
2. Figuratively, the word evokes anything that wounds, pricks, or causes suffering, like the thorn itself in Scripture — a symbol of pain and punishment. The crown of thorns thus embodies the ignominy and suffering that Jesus endured for us.
G0174.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἄκανθα (akantha, "thorn") and the suffix -ινος (-inos) which creates an adjective meaning "of the nature of." The thorn was well known in the Mediterranean as a symbol of pain and curse. In Hebrew, the word סִיר (sîr, "thorn") appears in the Old Testament to describe the thorns of the desert and divine punishments.
G0174.emploi: The word ἀκάνθινος appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the Passion narrative: in Mark 15:17 and John 19:5. These two evangelists report the incident where soldiers weave a crown of thorns and place it on Jesus' head while mocking him. The usage is strictly historical and narrative: it describes a real and concrete object — an instrument of torture — while carrying a major symbolic charge: that of innocent suffering and the contempt inflicted on the Son of God. The adjective emphasizes the raw and brutal aspect of the act.
G0174.portee: The crown of thorns reveals both the extreme humiliation that Jesus suffered and his sacrificial love. It reminds the Christian that Christ willingly bore the pain and shame in our place. Meditating on this detail — these thorns piercing the brow of the King — invites us to recognize the extent of his humiliation and compassion for sinners.

sens: That does not bear fruit or produce anything
That yields no results, no useful effect
That remains empty of meaning or effectiveness
That remains inactive, unproductive in the life of faith
G0175.detail:
1. In its literal sense, the word describes a plant or tree that does not produce fruit — it is the opposite of fertility. The Bible uses this imagery to speak of the Word of God: in Matthew 13:22 and Mark 4:19, Jesus says that the Word becomes "unfruitful" when worries and riches choke it within us, like thorns that prevent a plant from growing and bearing its spiritual fruit.
2. The word also designates what produces no results or useful effect. In Ephesians 5:11, Paul calls us to reject the "unfruitful works of darkness" — acts that lead to nothing good, that bear no spiritual fruit.
3. Applied to intellect or knowledge, "unfruitful" means empty, without productivity. In 1 Corinthians 14:14, Paul says that praying in tongues without understanding leaves the spirit in prayer but renders the mind "barren" — without fruit for the listener or for oneself.
4. Finally, the word characterizes an existence that remains inactive or idle despite God's gift. In 2 Peter 1:8, having Christian virtues "in abundance" prevents us from being "barren" in the knowledge of the Lord — it expresses spiritual and moral productivity.
G0175.origine: The Greek word ἄ-καρπος is composed of the prefix "a-" (absence, deprivation) and the word "karpos" (fruit). In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, similar terms related to the idea of sterility and lack of production can be found. The word conveys the classic biblical image of fruit: what a plant produces, and by extension, what a life, a word, a work produces.
G0175.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, always in a figurative sense — never to describe a plant in the literal sense. The first three uses (Matthew, Mark, 1 Corinthians) are applied to the Word, prayer, or understanding: they express the idea that grace, prayer, or instruction can remain ineffective or without benefit. The last four uses (Ephesians, Titus, 2 Peter, Jude) broaden the scope: the Christian's works, knowledge, and entire life must bear fruit. The word nuances its meaning according to the context: sometimes it is the Word that is rendered unfruitful by our worries, sometimes the works of darkness that remain unfruitful, sometimes our understanding or wisdom that remains barren due to lack of growth.
G0175.portee: This word invites the believer to examine their life: is the Word of God effective in them, or do worries and riches choke it? It pushes us to seek a productive life that bears spiritual and moral fruit — an existence that does not remain idle but manifests the virtues of Christ. It also warns us: rejecting the unfruitful works of darkness is choosing a life of fruit rather than a vain life.

sens: That cannot be blamed or criticized justly
That gives no grounds for accusation
Whose conduct is correct, without obvious defect
G0176.detail:
1. The Greek word "blameless" designates what cannot be justly accused or condemned: it is something or someone that does not deserve reproach. In Titus 2:8, Paul speaks of a "sound speech" that must be "blameless," meaning that our teaching or way of speaking must be so correct that no opponent can attack us by saying it is wrong or false.
2. More broadly, it describes a flawless conduct: something that gives no valid reason for criticism. When our speech is blameless, even our enemies find nothing to criticize, as there is no real defect to reproach. It is the opposite of a life or discourse that would offer grounds for malice.
G0176.origine: The Greek word is composed of three elements: the prefix "a-" meaning "not" or "without," the prefix "kata-" which intensifies the meaning, and the root "gignôskô" which means "to know" or "to judge." The basic idea is therefore "not knowable in evil," meaning that one cannot find in someone something bad that deserves condemnation. It is a rare word, coined to express the total absence of detectable guilt.
G0176.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 2:8. Paul uses it in a context of pastoral instructions: he asks Titus to ensure that the teaching is "sound" and "blameless." The goal is that in the face of this correct word, the opponents of the Church "may be ashamed" because they will have no valid argument to attack it. The word emphasizes the importance of integrity in the Christian testimony: our life and our words must be so blameless that even our critics find nothing to say against it.
G0176.portee: This word reminds Christians of the importance of leading a life and testimony without apparent defect, not to be just in the eyes of God (which is the work of grace), but so that no one can discredit the Gospel by justly accusing us. Living blamelessly is a form of respect towards God and wisdom for the mission: it neutralizes criticism and allows others to hear the message without distraction.

sens: That is not covered with a veil
Whose head is not covered
That manifests openly, without concealment
G0177.detail:
1. The word literally designates something that is not veiled, that has no covering. In 1 Corinthians 11:5, Paul speaks of a woman who prays or prophesies "with her head uncovered": her head is exposed, without the veil that Jewish and Mediterranean custom required.
2. By extension, this means that the head is uncovered, complete visibility. It is the state contrary to wearing a veil, which was a sign of respect and social order in the early Christian assemblies.
3. In a broader sense, the word can evoke what is revealed or manifested without a veil, which opposes what is hidden or concealed.
G0177.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "α" (privative, meaning "without") and "κατακαλύπτω" (to cover completely, to veil). The root "καλύπτω" fundamentally means "to cover." Thus, "ἀκατακάλυπτος" literally means "not covered," hence "uncovered." In the Greek Old Testament, this word corresponds to the Hebrew פָּרוּע (porua), which also means "uncovered" or "with disheveled hair," a term used to describe disorder and mourning.
G0177.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 1 Corinthians 11:5 and 13. Paul addresses the issue of veiling among women in Christian assemblies. In 1 Corinthians 11:5, he states a principle: a woman who prays or prophesies without a veil dishonors her head (God or her husband according to interpretations). In 1 Corinthians 11:13, he asks the Corinthians to judge for themselves whether it is proper for a woman to pray without a veil. In these two contexts, the word describes the absence of head covering and serves as a starting point for reflection on order, respect, and community in worship.
G0177.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible takes seriously the customs and signs that structure community life. The passage from 1 Corinthians 11 invites us to reflect on what order, respect, and dignity mean in our assemblies, beyond the details of attire. It pushes us to seek the eternal principle beneath the temporal practice: how do we honor God and one another in our worship?

sens: without prior judgment
without regular trial
without established verdict
G0178.detail:
1. The word denotes the absence of legal judgment or condemnation before an action. When Paul tells the magistrates of Ephesus that they have beaten him "without condemnation" (Acts 16:37), he protests: they whipped him publicly without first judging or condemning him. This is a violation of Roman law, which protected citizens against arbitrary punishments.

2. More broadly, the word expresses the idea of an action undertaken without a regular trial. When Paul asks the centurion: "Is it lawful for you to scourge a Roman citizen who is not even condemned?" (Acts 22:25), he raises the same injustice: one cannot punish someone except after a legitimate judgment, not before.
G0178.origine: The word is composed of three parts: the negation "a-" (there is not), "kata-" (against, according to), and "kritos" (judged, from the verb to judge). The base verb "katakrinô" means "to condemn" in a legal sense. The word belongs to the family of Greek terms related to justice and judgment; it implies the existence of a regular trial and an official sentence.
G0178.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, both in Acts, in the last two chapters of the account of Paul imprisoned in Jerusalem. In both cases, Paul uses it to protest against brutal treatment inflicted without legal grounds: first against the magistrates of Philippi who whipped him without trial (16:37), then to the centurion who is about to scourge him without waiting for the outcome of the ongoing judgment (22:25). It is a call for respect for Roman law and the dignity of the citizen.
G0178.portee: This word reminds us that Christian and civil justice requires respect for regular procedures and fundamental rights. Even in the face of injustice and persecution, Paul insists on respect for the law and legal order. He shows that the Gospel does not deny Christians the right to defend their dignity and rights guaranteed by the law, and that hasty judgment or accusation without trial contradicts justice.

sens: That cannot be dissolved, destroyed, or annulled
That lasts forever without end or degradation
That cannot be repealed or abolished (referring to a law or authority)
G0179.detail:
1. The word first describes what cannot be physically broken or annihilated: something so solid, so durable that no force can disintegrate it. It is the image of a chain or a bond that cannot be broken.

2. More broadly, it denotes what escapes time and destruction: what is not subject to death, degradation, or forgetfulness. In Hebrews 7:16, Paul uses it to describe the life of the risen Christ, a life that cannot come to an end.

3. It also applies to what cannot be annulled or revoked: a charge, a function, a power established permanently and irrevocably. Christ, in this passage, possesses a priesthood that nothing can abolish, unlike that of the Levitical priests who succeed one another and disappear.
G0179.origine: The word is composed of the privative prefix "a" (meaning "not," "without") and "katalutos," which comes from the verb "kataluo" (to dissolve, destroy, annul). The same root produces "catechesis" (ongoing instruction) and various words expressing destruction or dissolution. The basic idea is that of something that cannot be untied, broken, or annulled.
G0179.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 7:16. It characterizes the life of Christ as high priest: while the priests of the Old Covenant were many successors who died and gave way, Jesus possesses a priesthood based on an "imperishable life." It is a legal and theological term: it is not only that Christ lives eternally, but that His power as high priest cannot be revoked or transferred. This word emphasizes the uniqueness and permanence of Jesus' ministry.
G0179.portee: This word reminds the believer of the absolute stability of salvation in Christ. While everything human and earthly passes, is destroyed, or changes, the priesthood of Jesus is definitive and unshakeable. It guarantees an eternal intercession and a union with God that can never be broken.

sens: That cannot stop, that does not cease
That always wants more, never satisfied
That continuously pursues the object of its desire
G0180.detail:
1. The word first denotes what cannot stop or be stopped: an action, a desire, or a need that continues without end. It is the image of a thirst or hunger that is never quenched, always demanding more. In 2 Peter 2:14, false teachers have "insatiable eyes for sin": they constantly look at what leads them to evil, never satisfied or discouraged.
2. More broadly, the word describes an appetite or covetousness that knows no limits or brakes. Insatiability is a trait of the heart that always wants more: more pleasure, more wealth, more power. It is a form of spiritual blindness where one thinks that the next sin will finally fulfill them.
G0180.origine: The word comes from the Greek "kata-paustos" (that which stops) preceded by the negative prefix "a-" (not). At the root is "paustos," which means "stop" or "rest," related to the idea of ceasing. The Greek word translates the Hebrew that expresses the lack of limit, the impossibility of being satisfied. It is the opposite of rest and satisfaction.
G0180.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:14. Peter uses it to describe false teachers and seducers who live without restraint or moderation. This unique usage shows that insatiability is a sign of moral corruption: it characterizes one who has lost control of their desires and has made it their nature. It is a warning against the lifestyle of the wicked.
G0180.portee: This word reminds us that sin, far from satisfying us, chains us to an endless desire. Insatiability is not a strength, but a weakness and a spiritual prison. For the Christian, recognizing this dynamic helps us see the true face of temptation: it promises satisfaction but delivers only thirst. True and lasting satisfaction comes only from God.

sens: Absence of stability, instability
Confusion, chaos, lack of organization
Disturbance, agitation of the mind or circumstances
Tumult, revolt, public uprising
Moral or spiritual disturbance in a community
G0181.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the absence of stability or established order. When Paul asserts that "God is not a God of disorder, but of peace" (1 Corinthians 14:33), he speaks of the instability that reigns when everyone speaks at the same time without structure: a total lack of organization.

2. In public and political circumstances, the word means confusion and chaos: Jesus warns his disciples that they will hear of "uprisings" (Luke 21:9), that is, revolts and social upheavals where public order collapses.

3. Disorder also describes a state of personal or collective turmoil, such as the tribulations Paul enumerates: "troubles," "hardships," "imprisonments" (2 Corinthians 6:5) — the constant agitation that disturbs the heart and existence.

4. On a moral and spiritual level, disorder characterizes a Christian community where strife and bitterness prevail: "For where there is jealousy and selfish ambition, there will be disorder and every vile practice" (James 3:16), for the absence of peace opens the door to all evils.
G0181.origine: The word comes from the Greek root meaning "not in order," "not arranged." It is formed from the privative prefix "a" (which negates) and the word that denotes order, stable arrangement. The underlying Hebrew speaks of what is scattered or dispersed, an idea close to that of division and fragmentation.
G0181.emploi: The word appears five times in Greek in the New Testament, always to describe either external instability (wars, uprisings) or internal troubles within a person or a community. Paul uses it twice to speak of ecclesiastical problems: first in his call for order during gatherings (1 Corinthians 14:33), then when he enumerates the perils he has faced and fears to find among the Corinthians (2 Corinthians 6:5 and 12:20). James uses it to show how spiritual discord produces moral disorder (James 3:16). Luke uses it in the plural form ("uprisings") in the eschatological context of signs before the end (Luke 21:9). The word thus has nuances: sometimes external and political disorder, sometimes ecclesiastical or moral turmoil.
G0181.portee: This word reminds the believer that disorder — whether external or internal, political or spiritual — does not belong to God, but to the world in rupture with Him. Paul uses it to exhort the churches to cultivate order and peace rather than confusion: it is an invitation to examine how our quarrels, lack of self-control, and impatience cause trouble around us. Conversely, recognizing that God is a God of peace becomes a call to bring order, harmony, and stability into our relationships and communities.

sens: Lacking stability, changing constantly
Not keeping resolutions
Cannot be controlled, tamed (for the tongue)
G0182.detail: 1. The word describes what is unstable, without a fixed foundation, tossed about in every direction. James 1:8 applies it to the man "unstable in all his ways": this is someone who doubts, who wavers between two thoughts, like a wave driven by the wind. 2. It is moral inconstancy: the inability to maintain a direction, a resolution, a promise. A divided heart cannot ask anything of God with assurance. 3. In James 3:8, the word takes the form "that cannot be restrained" — the tongue is such an unstable, unpredictable evil, so difficult to control, that no human effort can truly master it. It is less about inconstancy than untamability, the total absence of possible control.
G0182.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to establish, to set in place" (hence "standing, stable"). The privative prefix "a-" negates it: "not established, not stable." It is the image of a house without a foundation, a person without footing, a tongue without restraint.
G0182.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, both times in the epistle of James, which focuses on the coherence of the Christian life. In James 1:8, it qualifies the man who asks with inconstancy, the heart divided between faith and doubt: he can obtain nothing from the Lord. In James 3:8, applied to the tongue, it emphasizes its uncontrollable, unstable, unpredictable nature — an evil that men cannot tame, despite all their efforts.
G0182.portee: This word invites the believer to examine his heart: am I unstable in my prayer, divided between faith and doubt? It is a warning against double-mindedness. For the tongue, it is a call to humility: we can only master it if the Holy Spirit governs our heart. Only a stable communion with God can produce stable speech.

sens: The field where Judas met his death after his betrayal
Symbol of the price of spilled blood and the condemnation of sin
G0184.detail:
1. Hakeldama is the Aramaic name of a field located near Jerusalem, traditionally located south of the Valley of Hinnom. Its name literally means "field of blood." After Judas' death, the apostles and disciples in Jerusalem named this field to commemorate the drama: it is there that the consequence of betrayal was fulfilled (Acts 1:19).
2. The field of blood symbolizes guilt and divine judgment on sin. The spilled blood — that of Jesus betrayed — forever marks this place, reminding us that the thirty pieces of silver paid for this betrayal have an exorbitant price in the eyes of God.
G0184.origine: Hakeldama is an Aramaic word (the language spoken by the Judeans at the time of Jesus), composed of "hakel" (field) and "dama" (blood). Luke, in writing Acts, reports this name in its original language to show that the inhabitants of Jerusalem themselves named this field, thus confirming the authenticity and gravity of the event.
G0184.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 1:19. Luke mentions this field when recounting how the disciples, after the Ascension, gathered in Jerusalem and decided to replace Judas among the apostles. The evangelist specifies that all the inhabitants of Jerusalem knew this field and understood why it was called that — proof that the event was notorious and that the name had become ingrained in collective memory.
G0184.portee: Hakeldama confronts us with the reality of divine judgment on sin. It is a reminder that betrayal has a price that no amount of money can erase. This field of blood invites us to meditate on the incomparable value of the blood of Jesus shed for our redemption, in stark contrast to the blood of the one who betrayed Him.

sens: Without mixture, uncorrupted
Free from malice or deceit
Innocent, guileless, devoid of guilt
G0185.detail:
1. The word first conveys the idea of an unmixed substance, pure — like gold without alloy. In Matthew 10:16, Jesus asks his disciples to be "wise as serpents and innocent as doves," indicating a purity of intention and action, without hidden deceit.

2. It then describes one who does not seek to deceive, who does not scheme. In Romans 16:19, Paul urges Christians to be "innocent in what is evil" — that is, not to cultivate it in secret, not to handle it as an instrument of deceit.

3. By extension, it qualifies moral innocence: in Philippians 2:15, being "blameless and pure" means living without visible guilt, without justified reproach, shining with a transparent righteousness amidst a corrupt world.
G0185.origine: The word comes from a root meaning "to mix" (κεράννυμι); the negative prefix α- reverses the meaning: "without mixture." It is thus the image of physical purity (a liquid undiluted, a metal without alloy) applied to moral conduct. The root speaks of mixing, hence the idea that being ἀκέραιος is to refuse any compromise, any suspicious mixture in one's behavior.
G0185.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always to exhort believers to moral integrity. Matthew 10:16 contrasts it with the cunning of serpents: the disciple must combine prudence with a lack of malice. Romans 16:19 uses it to urge purity concerning evil — not to ignore it naively, but not to participate in it. Philippians 2:15 places it in a broader picture: the Church, pure and blameless, must shine with righteousness in a morally compromised generation. It is always a quality expected of the believer.
G0185.portee: This word calls the Christian to transparent integrity: neither naivety (hence the "wisdom" of the serpent), nor duplicity. It is an ideal of moral frankness — absence of hidden calculation, lies, or shameful compromise. In the face of a world that mixes good and evil, the believer is called to remain pure, not out of ignorance, but by a deliberate choice of honesty.

sens: That does not bend, that does not yield
That remains firm in the face of obstacles or suffering
That remains constant in faith and commitments
G0186.detail:
1. The word literally describes something that cannot be bent or curved — a firmness, a rigidity that resists all pressure. It is the image of wood that does not bend, or a position that cannot be swayed. In Hebrews 10:23, Paul speaks of holding "unswervingly" (unshakeable) to the confession of our hope: we must hold firm, without bending under doubt or fear.
2. The word applies to moral and spiritual constancy, to the ability to stand firm when everything pushes to abandon. It evokes the stability of a mountain in the face of storms: it cannot be shaken. Hebrews 10:23 invites believers to keep their confidence in God and His promise unshakeable, despite the trials of the present.
G0186.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb κλίνω (klínô) which means "to bend, to curve, to incline" — think of a stem that bends in the wind. The prefix ἀ- (a-) negates this action: ἀκλινής thus means "that cannot be bent." It is a rare word, constructed to express absolute firmness, a refusal to bend under pressure.
G0186.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Hebrews 10:23, where Paul exhorts Christians to hold "unshakeable" the confession (the public affirmation) of their hope. In this context, it is a pastoral exhortation: in the face of the temptations of apostasy and the trials faced by the early Hebrew Christians, Paul calls them to a faithfulness that does not waver, that does not capitulate. The word emphasizes a calm and serene determination, rooted in God.
G0186.portee: For the Christian, this word invites absolute and concrete trust: faith is not a vague feeling, but a firm commitment that nothing should shake. It speaks to those going through trials or doubts — they are called to stand firm, without being diverted from their confession in Jesus. It is a call to spiritual maturity and perseverance.

sens: To reach full maturity (referring to a harvest, fruits)
To be at the time of harvest or vintage
To be ready, completed, accomplished
G0187.detail:
1. The word describes the moment when a harvest has reached its full maturity and is ready to be picked. It is the state of complete maturity of fruits. In Revelation 14:18, the grapes of the earth "are ripe": the image is of clusters swollen with juice, golden or red, ready to be harvested.
2. More broadly, the word applies to anything that has reached its crucial moment, its fulfillment. It expresses the idea that the time has come, that the process is complete and action must follow. The ripe harvest does not wait: it demands to be gathered immediately.
3. Spiritually, in Revelation, this maturity of the grapes symbolizes the completion of God's plan, the moment when judgment must be fulfilled — the time is no longer to let rot or wait, but to act.
G0187.origine: The Greek word comes from the root ἀκμή (acmè: the peak, the summit, the apogee). It is formed on the image of the culminating point. The verbal suffix transforms this idea of peak into action: "to reach its peak." In Hebrew, the Old Testament often uses verbs related to maturity (like בשׁל, bashal: to cook, to ripen) for similar realities, but ἀκμάζω particularly emphasizes reaching the point of perfection.
G0187.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 14:18. John uses it in a vision of the final judgment: an angel bearing a sickle asks another angel to begin the harvest of the grapes of the earth, for they "are ripe." The context is one of eschatological urgency — the time set by God has come, action can no longer be delayed. The word concretely translates the physical state of the fruit to express the fulfillment of divine timing.
G0187.portee: This word reminds the reader that God sets times, that nothing escapes His plan, and that the fulfillment of judgment cannot be postponed indefinitely. It also evokes that every era, every life, has its moment of "ripeness" where action becomes inevitable: it is an invitation to be aware of the present time, of the seriousness of the hour we live in.

sens: At this present moment, right now, at this moment
G0188.detail: 1. The word designates the current moment, the instant unfolding before our eyes: it is now, at this precise instant. In Matthew 15:16, Jesus is astonished that His disciples, after all His teaching and all the miracles they have witnessed, are "still" without understanding — that is, up to the very moment He speaks, until now, they have not understood.
G0188.origine: The Greek word comes from ἀκμή (akmé), which literally denotes the point or peak of something — the sharp edge of a weapon, the culminating moment. Used here in the accusative in an adverbial sense, it freezes time at its extreme point, the present moment in all its sharpness.
G0188.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 15:16. Jesus has just explained to the crowds that defilement comes from within, from the heart of man; the disciples ask Him for an explanation of His parable. Jesus' question emphasizes the present moment, almost with a slight tender exasperation: how is it that "still" now, after all this time spent together, they do not grasp it?
G0188.portee: This word invites the reader not to remain in misunderstanding, but to seize the present moment to seek the truth of God. It also suggests that hardening or lack of understanding is never inevitable — there remains time to learn and to transform.

sens: the ability to perceive sounds, the auditory sense
the ear, the physical organ of hearing
that which is heard: a message, a teaching
fame, what is said about someone
G0189.detail:
1. Hearing is the natural faculty that allows the body to perceive sounds. Paul uses it to compare the different functions of the body: "If the whole body were an eye, where would be the hearing?" (1 Corinthians 12:17). It is a vital ability among others.

2. The word also refers to the physical organ, the ear itself. When Jesus heals, "they brought to him the deaf and those who had difficulty speaking; and he healed them": hearing was restored (Mark 7:35). It is the concrete instrument through which sounds are received.

3. Hearing can also refer to the message that is heard, particularly teaching or preaching. Paul writes: "You received the word of God, which we made you hear" (1 Thessalonians 2:13), where "hear" means to receive the transmitted teaching. The Epistle to the Hebrews speaks of those who "are not spiritually mature" and "have difficulty hearing" the Word (Hebrews 5:11).

4. Finally, hearing can mean fame, what is said: "His fame spread throughout all Syria" (Matthew 4:24). It is the reputation that spreads by word of mouth.
G0189.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to hear" (akouō). Hearing is the action or faculty of listening, hence its direct link to auditory perception. In Greek, this term often translates the Hebrew word "to hear" (shama'), which in biblical Hebrew means not only to perceive by the ear but also to obey, understand, and welcome. This nuance sheds light on why the Bible associates listening with understanding and acceptance of the Word of God.
G0189.emploi: The word "hearing" appears about 22 times in the New Testament, in various contexts. It can refer to the physical sense of hearing (1 Corinthians 12:17, 2 Peter 2:8), the auditory organ itself (Mark 7:35, Acts 28:26), or the received message, especially the Gospel and Christian teaching (1 Thessalonians 2:13, Hebrews 4:2). Very often, it takes on the meaning related to preaching or the transmission of the Word: in Galatians 3:2, 3:5, it refers to the call to faith received through preaching. It can also express fame or reputation, what spreads from mouth to mouth (Matthew 4:24, Mark 1:28, Matthew 14:1). This diversity shows that the Greek word covers both physical sensation and its metaphorical use for the spiritual reception of the Word.
G0189.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that faith comes by hearing the Word of God: "Faith comes from what is heard" (Romans 10:17). But it also invites to true listening, which is not limited to perceiving sounds — it is a reception that engages understanding and obedience. By speaking of those who have "ears to hear" (Matthew 13:14), Jesus emphasizes that hearing is spiritually useful only if accompanied by discernment and acceptance.

sens: to walk behind someone
to go with someone from one place to another
to obey someone, to put oneself at their service
to be a disciple, to accept the teaching and authority of a master
G0190.detail:
1. In the literal sense, it means to walk behind someone, to follow in their footsteps: the crowd follows Jesus on foot after seeing him in Capernaum (Matthew 14:13), or the people follow him after the multiplication of the loaves (John 6:2). It is to be physically behind a person.

2. By extension, it means to accompany someone in their movements, to share their path: Peter follows Jesus from a distance during the trial (Luke 22:54), the women follow him to Calvary (Mark 15:41).

3. The word takes on a sense of obedience and dependence: the sheep of the good Shepherd follow him because they know his voice (John 10:4, 10:27). It is to recognize someone's authority and submit to it.

4. Finally, "to follow" means to be a disciple, to accept a master's call to share in their life and teaching: when Jesus says to Peter, "Follow me," he invites him to become his disciple (Matthew 4:20). It is the deepest commitment, touching on faith and the whole existence.
G0190.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "the road, the way" (related to κέλευθος). It primarily designates one who walks on the same road. In the Greek Old Testament, it generally translates the Hebrew verb הָלַךְ ("to go," "to walk"), especially in the expression "to go after" (הָלַךְ אָהֲרֵי). This image of the road traveled together becomes the natural expression of the disciple-master relationship in Jesus' teaching.
G0190.emploi: The verb appears 86 times in the New Testament, especially in the four Gospels, where it is central to the description of Jesus' ministry. It first describes the crowds that follow Jesus out of curiosity or need for healing (Matthew 4:25, Mark 3:7). But its decisive meaning is that of the call to discipleship: Jesus calls Matthew (Luke 5:27), Peter and Andrew (Matthew 4:20), and each time "to follow" means to leave one's old life to live in communion with the Master. The word is also used in the sense of moral imitation: in Mark 8:34 and parallels, Jesus asks those who want to be his disciples to deny their own interests and follow him. In Acts and the epistles, it becomes rarer but retains its significance: to follow Jesus is to cling to him forever (John 13:36-37).
G0190.portee: For the Christian reader, "to follow" Jesus is not a mere theoretical adherence: it is a movement of the heart and life. This word reminds us that faith is a concrete walk, a road to be traveled each day alongside Christ. To follow means to accept his authority, to obey his voice like the sheep to the shepherd (John 10:27), and to renounce oneself to live according to his teaching. It is the invitation to conversion, renewed in every generation of believers.

sens: Perceive sounds through the ear
Listen attentively, pay attention to
Learn news, be informed about
Understand the meaning of a word, grasp the message
Obey, take into account what is heard
Respond favorably to a prayer
G0191.detail:
1. To hear is primarily to perceive sounds through the physical ear: this is the simplest and most concrete meaning of the word (Matthew 13:16: "Blessed are your eyes, for they see; and your ears, for they hear").

2. However, to hear also means to listen voluntarily, to give attention to what is being said. Jesus calls those who want to understand: "He who has ears to hear, let him hear" (Mark 4:23), which means: really focus, welcome this message.

3. To hear can simply mean to learn news, to be informed: when King Herod learns of the child's birth, he "heard it said" that Jesus was going to Jerusalem (Matthew 2:3; John 12:12). This is receiving information by hearsay.

4. To hear also means to understand the deeper meaning, to grasp the spiritual message, not just the words. That is why Jesus explains that some "hear" the word but receive it poorly (Mark 4:18), while others listen and keep it (Luke 11:28).

5. Hearing often implies a reaction: to obey. When the prophets say, "Hear the word of the Lord," they are asking not only to listen but to obey. This relates to the Hebrew שׁמע (shama'), which means both to hear and to obey.

6. When speaking of God, to hear also means to respond, to answer: John 9:31 says that God "does not hear sinners," literally "does not hear the sinners." This means He responds to the prayer of those who fear Him.
G0191.origine: The Greek word ἀκούω comes from an ancient root related to auditory perception. In biblical Hebrew and Aramaic, it primarily translates the verb שׁמע (shama'), which means not only to "hear" physically but also to "listen with obedience," even to "obey." This semantic richness of the Hebrew word is reflected in the Greek usage: to hear is not passive; it is a voluntary act. The Greek word has given rise in French to the words "acoustique" (related to sound) and "audience" (those who listen).
G0191.emploi: The word ἀκούω is one of the most frequent in the New Testament: 401 occurrences. It appears everywhere, from the Gospels to the apostolic letters. Sometimes it simply describes the act of perceiving a sound or a voice (Matthew 13:16), while at other times it expresses learning news (Matthew 2:3: Herod learns of the Messiah's arrival). Very often, it is used in the parables and teachings of Jesus to signify spiritual listening — the kind that changes the heart. Mark 4:3-23 illustrates this well: "Listen! A sower went out" asks not just to hear words but to welcome the Word. In Acts, the verb appears when Peter and John report what they have heard (Acts 17:21: the Athenians were only seeking to "hear" news). Hebrews 3:15 echoes the call of the Psalm: "If you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts," where hearing calls for conversion. The nuance also changes depending on the complement: to hear "from" someone is to receive their teaching; to hear "that" is to learn news.
G0191.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that faith comes from hearing: "Faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes from the word of Christ" (Romans 10:17). Hearing the Word of God is not passive: it is an act of the soul that engages our entire life. Jesus constantly calls to "truly hear," beyond physical ears — to welcome His message into the heart to obey. It is a call to conversion and personal transformation.

sens: Lack of self-control, inability to restrain oneself
Debauchery, excess in bodily pleasures
Loss of control in the face of desires
G0192.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the absence of power over oneself, the inability to curb one's impulses. It is a weakness of will in the face of what one desires. In Matthew 23:25, Jesus reproaches the Pharisees for their hearts being filled with intemperance: they allow themselves to be dominated by their unrestrained desires.
2. Concretely, intemperance manifests itself through excess in the satisfaction of pleasures — eating, drinking, or in the sexual realm. It is the absence of balance and moderation. In 1 Corinthians 7:5, Paul speaks of incontinence as a temptation of the devil: when spouses deprive each other for a long time, the lack of self-control may expose them to commit infidelity.
3. Beyond actions, the word describes an inner state: that of someone who has lost control of their desires and whose reason no longer governs their passions.
G0192.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and literally means "without strength" or "without power" (a- = without, and kratos = strength, power). Intemperance is thus the absence of that masterful power that should reign in the soul. It is the opposite of enkrateia, self-control or mastery over oneself. In Hebrew, this idea was expressed by other terms, notably those evoking overflow or drunkenness of the heart.
G0192.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Matthew 23:25, in Jesus' critical discourse against the Pharisees, it describes the inner vice that fills their hearts despite their outward piety. In 1 Corinthians 7:5, Paul uses it in an ethical and practical context: he advises spouses not to prolong sexual abstinence beyond what is beneficial, as this could expose them to incontinence — that is, to succumbing to the temptation of infidelity. In both cases, it is a vice that threatens the people of God and to which believers must resist by grace.
G0192.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that true victory is not primarily external or apparent, but internal: it is the mastery of desires and passions. The Bible does not hide that this mastery is difficult; it requires vigilance, prayer, and the help of the Holy Spirit. That is why Paul warns: allowing our passions to run unchecked exposes us to temptation. Intemperance is not just a matter of morality, but of freedom — for one who does not master oneself becomes a slave to their desires.

sens: Lacking the strength to dominate oneself
Having no self-control, particularly in appetites and desires
Acting without restraint or moral control
G0193.detail: 1. The word first evokes a weakness or inner impotence: it is not having the strength (the "kratê", the inner power) to master oneself. 2. Applied to morality, it describes one who cannot restrain themselves, who is a slave to their desires and impulses. In 2 Timothy 3:3, Paul lists the traits of the last days: "without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, intemperate, fierce" — the intemperate is ranked alongside those who have lost all self-control and all ethics.
G0193.origine: The word comes from the root "kratéô" (to have power, to dominate) with the prefix "a-" which negates it: intemperate = without power over oneself, without mastery. It is the opposite of one who possesses "enkrateia" (self-control, mastery over oneself). In Proverbs 27:20, it translates a Hebrew term describing someone without measure or moderation.
G0193.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: 2 Timothy 3:3. Paul depicts the men of the last days as "lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy, without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, intemperate, fierce." Intemperance thus figures in a portrait of total moral decay, where the absence of self-control is a symptom of a rupture with God and with all virtue.
G0193.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that self-control is not a weakness or oppression, but a strength: that of dominating one's appetites instead of being enslaved by them. Intemperance is presented as a mark of distance from God. In contrast, the fruit of the Spirit includes "temperance" (Galatians 5:23), which is precisely this regained power to govern oneself.

sens: Undiluted wine, poured pure
Divine wrath poured out without temperance or softening
G0194.detail:
1. The word properly designates wine poured without mixture — among the Greeks, wine was usually mixed with water, and drinking pure wine was an excessive act or a mark of fury. In Revelation 14:10, it refers to the "wine of the fury of God, poured without mixture into the cup of His wrath": the image evokes punishment poured out in all its strength, without any mitigation.
2. Figuratively, "without mixture" denotes divine wrath in all its purity and absolute intensity — it is not softened by any mercy, any reserve. It is a complete and uncompromising judgment.
G0194.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb κεράννυμι (to pour, to mix) preceded by the prefix α- (negation): literally "not mixed." The root evokes the action of mixing ingredients — here, its absence. The Greek Old Testament translates the Hebrew חֲמַר (wine) and חֵמָה (fury) with this term, both words conveying the idea of vigor and violence.
G0194.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 14:10. John uses it to describe the final judgment reserved for those who worship the Beast: the wine of divine wrath poured "without mixture" symbolizes total punishment, without reduction or mitigation. This apocalyptic image expresses the idea that divine justice will be executed with absolute completeness, as decreed.
G0194.portee: This word reminds us that divine judgment, when it comes, suffers no mitigation for those who deserve it. For the Christian, it is a serious call to repentance and a reason for gratitude towards God's grace, which has saved us from this wrath through Christ.

sens: The quality of being precise, rigorous, without approximation
Meticulous mastery of a discipline or knowledge
Strict observance of a rule or doctrine
G0195.detail: 1. Accuracy is the quality of being precise and error-free, not deviating by an iota from the goal. It is accounting for things as they truly are, without adding or subtracting anything. Paul uses this word to describe the teaching he received at the feet of Gamaliel: an "exact knowledge of the law" (Acts 22:3), meaning not just a superficial knowledge, but a precise and rigorous understanding, letter by letter, of what the Law prescribes. 2. Accuracy also speaks of the mastery acquired through meticulous study. Paul did not receive vague or approximate teaching, but rigorous learning from a renowned master, where every detail matters and doctrine is transmitted without distortion. 3. Finally, it implies strict observance: one who has this accuracy in the knowledge of the Law applies it scrupulously, without compromise, with the zeal that Paul himself manifested towards God at that time.
G0195.origine: The Greek word ἀκρίβεια comes from the adjective ἀκριβής (rigorous, precise), itself derived from a root meaning "point" or "extremity" — the idea is to go down to the smallest details, to the point of detail. The same root produces words meaning "with accuracy," "with rigor." In Hebrew, this concept appears notably in contexts where emphasis is placed on uprightness and stability (as in יַצִּיב in Daniel 7:16), qualities that demand flawless precision.
G0195.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 22:3, in the speech where Paul presents himself to the Jewish authorities in Jerusalem. He describes the rigorous rabbinical training he received: he was instructed "in the exact knowledge of the law of our fathers." This phrase emphasizes that Paul was not a mere passive listener, but a student subjected to a draconian learning process, where the precision of knowledge was crucial. It was precisely this training that once made him so zealous in persecuting Christians — he acted with the same rigor he had been taught. The word thus reveals how Paul understood his own commitment at that time: not an instinctive fervor, but a precise obedience to what he believed to be God's will.
G0195.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the difference between true knowledge and pseudo-knowledge. Paul had accuracy in the letter of the Law, but he lacked the understanding of Christ who fulfills all meaning in the Law. It reminds us that academic rigor and even religious fervor are not sufficient without the revelation and transformation of the heart. For the Christian, it is a call to seek in Scripture, not only formal accuracy but a living understanding of the one who is at the heart of all Scripture: Jesus Christ.

sens: that conforms rigorously to a rule, doctrine, principle
that tolerates no exception, no flexibility
G0196.detail:
1. This word describes what is conducted with absolute rigor, without deviation. Paul speaks of the "most strict" sect of Judaism (Acts 26:5), meaning the one that applied the Law with the most accuracy and inflexibility.
2. The word evokes a demand without compromise: it is the firmness of one who makes no concessions and who demands precise conformity to what he considers just or true.
G0196.origine: The word comes from a Greek root meaning "to break" or "to separate," hence the idea of a clear delimitation between what is correct and what is not. The comparative and superlative show increasing degrees of rigor: one can be strict, stricter, the strictest. The Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) uses it to translate the Hebrew meaning "firmly established" or "solid," emphasizing unshakeability.
G0196.emploi: This superlative appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 26:5. Paul defends himself before King Agrippa by asserting that he once followed the most rigorous Pharisaic sect. This passage shows how the Pharisees themselves were reputed for their uncompromising application of the Mosaic Law, to the point that "the most strict" of their sects represented the pinnacle of this demand. The word lends credibility to Paul's testimony: he speaks from experience, having lived this severity himself.
G0196.portee: This word reminds us that true piety does not consist of seeking loopholes or circumventing principles. But by reading the Pauline context (Paul recounts his journey to Jesus), it also shows that external rigor towards the Law, however admirable, does not equate to the inner transformation that only Christ can provide. It is an invitation to examine whether our obedience is formal or rooted in the love of God.

sens: With greater precision, rigor, or detail
By examining a question more thoroughly or meticulously
With greater attention to details or nuances
G0197.detail: 1. "More precisely" expresses a correction or a deepening: it revisits something to state it with more accuracy or clarity. Aquila and Priscilla teach Apollos "more precisely" the way of God (Acts 18:26), meaning they complete or rectify his teaching by making it more rigorous. 2. The word also denotes an examination or inquiry conducted with greater care. The Jews ask Lysias to bring Paul "as if [you] wanted to examine his case more precisely" (Acts 23:15), suggesting a desire to delve deeper into the matter. 3. "Precisely" can also qualify knowledge or discernment: Felix "knew quite precisely" what concerned the Christian message (Acts 24:22), meaning he understood it with sufficient accuracy.
G0197.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective ἀκριβής (akribès), which evokes a finesse of work, precision, and scrupulous accuracy. The root suggests the idea of something well-adjusted, without margin for error. This Greek term translates in several places the Hebrew יָטַב (yatab) or יְצֵב (yetsèb), which express correctness or solidity. It is a rare but precise word, reserved for contexts where accuracy truly matters.
G0197.emploi: The comparative ἀκριβέστερον (more precisely) appears four times in Acts, always to mark increased precision or correction. In Luke, who values historical details, this word highlights moments when the truth must be stated or examined without approximation. Aquila and Priscilla use it to enhance Apollos's understanding (18:26); the Jews use it in their cunning to reach Paul (23:15, 20); Felix employs it to describe his own knowledge of Christian doctrine (24:22). The context varies, but the meaning remains constant: it is about going beyond the surface, penetrating deeper.
G0197.portee: This word reminds us that truth deserves rigorous and straightforward attention. For the disciple, it invites not to settle for a superficial understanding of the Gospel, but to seek to grasp it "more precisely." Like Apollos, who accepts to be instructed "more precisely," the Christian must remain open to a deeper and more faithful knowledge of God's Word.

sens: To inquire from someone with attention and method
To seek to know the precise details of a matter
To verify facts carefully before acting
G0198.detail:
1. To inquire from someone with attention and method: this means asking questions to learn what they know. Herod does this with the Magi, asking them how long the star has been shining (Matthew 2:7) — he does not ask lightly, but wants to know a lot about this phenomenon.

2. To seek to know the precise details of a matter: the word does not refer to a simple request, but to the effort to discover exact and complete information. Herod inquires carefully about when the star appeared to calculate the age of the child announced to him.

3. To verify facts carefully before acting: this verb marks the approach of someone who wants to base their actions on reliable information. In Matthew 2:16, Herod has inquired carefully, then he acts — he kills the children according to the timeline he learned: it is the precise inquiry that precedes the decision.
G0198.origine: The word comes from the adjective *akribès*, which means "exact, precise, meticulous." The root evokes the idea of searching down to the details, leaving nothing to chance. It is a verb from a family rich in Greek: *akribèia* (exactness, rigor) appears several times in the New Testament, especially when Luke or Paul want to emphasize the precision of what they report.
G0198.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Matthew 2, in the scene of the Magi's visit to Herod. In Matthew 2:7, Herod "inquires carefully" of the Magi. In Matthew 2:16, we learn that it is according to "the date he had inquired carefully" that he sets his murderous plan in motion. In both cases, the emphasis is on meticulous, methodical information — Herod does not jump to conclusions hastily; he gathers facts precisely. It is this exactness that makes his crime all the more premeditated and heinous.
G0198.portee: This word shows us that Herod does not act out of simple instinctive jealousy, but by cold calculation: he investigates first, then strikes. This underscores the deliberate malice of one who rejects the child-king. For the Christian reader, it is a reminder that knowledge of the facts is not enough to justify us before God if our hearts are closed to His will — Herod "inquires carefully," but remains blind to the true light.

sens: With precision and without error
With care and attention to all details
In a meticulous and rigorous manner
G0199.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes factual precision, the absence of error or approximation. When Herod asks the Magi to go and seek information about the child Jesus "exactly" (Matthew 2:8), he wants them to report verified facts, not rumors. 2. It also expresses the careful attention given to a task. Luke writes that he has investigated "exactly" all the events from the beginning (Luke 1:3): he did not gather information haphazardly, but with method and vigilance. 3. In a moral or spiritual context, the word signifies rigor in conduct or teaching. Apollos teaches with "exactness" what concerns Jesus (Acts 18:25), even though he only knows the baptism of John: his discourse is careful and correct.
G0199.origine: The word comes from the adjective "akribès" (ακριβής), which literally means "narrow, tight, compact." The image is that of something well-adjusted, without slack or void: hence the meaning of "exact, precise, rigorous." The root evokes the idea of leaving nothing aside, being attentive to details.
G0199.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, mainly in narratives and moral instructions. Matthew uses it to demand factual precision (2:8). Luke chooses it to characterize his approach as a historian and researcher (1:3). Acts uses it to describe the quality of Apollos's teaching (18:25). Paul also uses it in his ethical exhortations (Ephesians 5:15: to live "exactly"). The word always emphasizes rigor, whether factual, methodical, or moral.
G0199.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that the Christian faith is based on verified facts (Luke investigates "exactly") and that authentic teaching is precise and careful. It also invites the believer to live with attention and vigilance, without negligence or spiritual approximation. It is a call to seriousness in the knowledge of Christ and in the Christian walk.
